Pacing AI via Compute Reallocation

Romeo Dean, Thomas Larsen · November 17th 2026

We offer a concrete proposal for pacing the frontier.

1. Transparency: Verified Compute Allocation Disclosures (VCAD)

[Figure: Example compute disclosure. Serving customers · 19% · Safeguard classifiers, · 4% · Capabilities R&D · 64% · Non-capabilities R&D, · 4% · Idle · 7% · trained on · 2%]

2. Reallocation: Shift compute away from capabilities R&D

The first component is Verified Compute Allocation Disclosures (VCAD): AI companies regularly disclose their compute usage, and an independent auditor verifies the disclosures. The second component is to reallocate compute away from capabilities R&D and toward other use cases, such as serving customers and safety research (non-capabilities R&D).

We roughly estimate that pacing via compute reallocation starting January 2027, with a 15% cap, would delay the intelligence explosion by a year. This is most likely insufficient to prevent AI takeover (or mitigate other problems created by RSI), and so this year should be used to implement a more durable policy regime such as Plan A or Plan S.

Nearly every approach to pacing, including ones built on safety and security requirements, strongly benefits from VCAD:

  • Any pacing proposal that actually slows down AI development must do so either by reducing one of the inputs to AI development (such as training compute, experiment compute, or automated or human labor), or by implementing a safeguard that results in using inputs less efficiently (e.g., avoiding neuralese).

  • Something like VCAD is evidently needed for compute restrictions. For other input restrictions and safeguards, VCAD is highly desirable to prevent attacks of the form “don’t follow this restriction/safeguard on some compute, and hide or misreport that compute.”

With VCAD, competitors and the public can trust a company that says it is pacing. As evidence of risk grows, this could enable a “race to the top”. If regulation later mandates pacing, a VCAD process that companies have already built and stress-tested makes that regulation faster to write and more workable.

Given the urgency of the situation, we elected to publish this relatively quickly. We are not very confident in any given detail of our proposal. Nevertheless, we think it represents a step forward in concreteness for pacing proposals and hope that we and others can quickly turn this into something workable.

VCAD Implementation Proposal

We propose that AI companies take the following steps to estimate and disclose their compute usage:

[Figure: Step 1, logging: workloads on GPUs go through logging infra into a database. Step 2, classification: capabilities vs. non-capabilities. Step 3, disclosure: a public disclosure. How AI companies could estimate compute usage

The basic proposal is:

Step 1: Logging. Implement logging infrastructure that logs all workloads running inside the AI company, along with relevant metadata.

Each company should create a database that accounts for all the compute (measured in GPU-hours) that the company uses (more detail on the scope here). Each entry in the table should have the GPU-hours used by the workload, and depending on which of the following categories of workload it fits into, it should have the following metadata attached to the log:

Workload TypeUserGPU TypeTime windowModelDataTranscriptFeeds into training?Other
R&DOwner✓✓Code & DatasetsPointers to (i) workloads & agents started by this process and (ii) the agent that started the job
External inferenceAPI Key / OAuth✓✓✓Tokens✓ iff not ZDR✓
Internal inferenceAPI Key✓✓✓Tokens✓ iff not ZDR✓Pointer to AI R&D jobs launched
MonitoringOwner✓✓✓Tokens✓ iff input not ZDRPointer to workloads it's monitoring

Step 2: Classification.

  1. Classify the logged jobs according to whether they contributed to capabilities R&D (detailed proposal here).

  2. Weight the jobs by how many quality-adjusted GPU-hours they used (detailed proposal here).

Step 2 involves three substages: 2.1) Aggregate GPU-hours. 2.2) Classify workloads into capabilities vs. non-capabilities. 2.3) Estimate idle compute.

2.1) Aggregate GPU-hours. Getting an overall estimate of compute use requires aggregating across heterogeneous GPUs into a single unified GPU-hr metric (e.g., “H100-equivalents”). We discuss this in more detail in an appendix.

2.2) Classify workloads into capabilities vs. non-capabilities, using a mixture of AI classification and manual human classification. By “capabilities” compute, we mean compute that has any positive capabilities effects — including work that has capabilities and safety externalities. This centrally includes:

  • Experiments to improve algorithms and data

  • Data generation or filtering

  • Training more capable AIs

  • Internal inference in service of the above

Unfortunately, it’s hard to give a crisp definition of this, and there are many edge cases. The exact definition isn’t that important so long as it isn’t possible to use internal non-capabilities compute in a way that has large capabilities externalities. We discuss this in more detail in a supplement here.

2.3) Estimate idle compute. By idle compute, we mean compute that is not turned on or is not in use. This includes:

  • Hot spares

  • Downtime

  • New racks that haven’t started use

When Step 2 is complete, the company will have an internal estimate of compute allocation such as the following:

[Figure. Example compute disclosure · Serving · customers · 19% · Safeguard · classifiers, 4% · Capabilities R&D · 64% · Non-capabilities R&D, 4% · Idle · 7% · trained on · 2%]

The categories are defined as follows:

  • Serving customers: compute used to serve customers, including via API, web interfaces (e.g., Claude.ai), and desktop (e.g., Claude Code). We also call this category “External Inference”.

    • The “trained on” box is the subset of external inference that feeds back into capabilities, either by being directly trained on, paraphrased and then trained on, or similar.

  • Safeguard classifiers: monitors checking for misuse

  • Internal Inference: inference compute used for internal AI company use. This includes evaluations, internal coding agents, and RL rollouts.

    • We subdivide internal inference into capabilities and safety, where safety compute refers to the internal inference that doesn’t have significant capabilities externalities.

  • Non-Capabilities R&D: R&D compute that has minimal capabilities externalities.

  • Capabilities R&D: all other R&D compute.

See Supplement C for more detail on the definitions.

Step 3: Disclosure. Publicly report a breakdown of how much compute was spent in each category, and whether it counted as capabilities (red) or non-capabilities.

The AI company publishes a disclosure of the compute allocation. We could imagine, for example, a disclosure every two weeks covering compute allocation over that period. This report should include:

  • An overall estimate of compute allocation

  • An overview of the methodology used to make and audit that estimate

  • An analysis of possible mistakes, discrepancies the auditor was not able to resolve, and an estimate of the error rate

  • Chip-conversion ratios

  • Descriptions of N (e.g., 30) non-capabilities projects, randomly sampled in proportion to compute

We recommend that AI companies publish this disclosure through a channel that punishes misreporting. As a starting point, it should be part of the company’s SB 53 frontier AI framework. As soon as possible, it should move to a channel with real liability, such as being included in financial disclosures or directly required by regulation with sufficient teeth to deter violation.

Even with improved reporting channels, there would still be risk of:

  • Deception from AI executives

  • Goodharting: for the attacks we’re most worried about, it can happen without explicit deception, particularly attack 5 (external compute) and attack 7 (misclassifying capabilities compute). We’d recommend these reports explicitly make claims about the company not doing activities in these buckets.

  • Internal conspiracies the leadership doesn’t know about.

Despite this, such a requirement would probably galvanize a lot of self-verification internally, because the CEO and board may want to be really sure they aren’t lying in these disclosures.

Third-party auditors (3PAs) would verify the integrity of this process. We give a baseline auditing process and a robust auditing process, and estimate the error rate for each.

Baseline Auditing

Baseline auditing involves checking (and potentially reproducing parts of) the accounting process, via:

  • Financial Auditing

  • Spot-check random workloads

  • Independent classification pipeline

  • …

The baseline auditing process:

  • Could be implemented today (it does not rely on new science).

  • Is sufficient to give an accurate estimate of compute allocation within AI companies today.

  • Is not sufficient to withstand adversarial pressure from a company trying to actively lie in their disclosure, which could happen under a pacing regime where companies are supposed to significantly limit compute used for capabilities.

It involves the following substages:

3.1 Completeness. Does the table include all the compute?

  • Check financial data to make sure that the total chip-hours being reported by the company match the amount of compute it should have, given its compute contracts.

  • Create a database of all datacenters used by the AI company with capacity information.

3.2 Database Integrity. Is the information in the table a correct accounting of workloads in the company?

  • Spot-check a random set of workloads to confirm that the metadata is consistent with the reported GPU-hrs, by estimating the compute requirements from the auditors’ best understanding of the stack. Optionally, this could be assisted by increased visibility into the compilers and performance of the live stack on different workloads.

  • Directly review the logging code to check for bugs and/or backdoors.

  • Check whether auditor-initiated workloads are logged correctly.

3.3 Classification. Is the mapping from the database to capabilities / non-capabilities being done correctly?[1]

  • Run an independent classification pipeline.

  • Manually review a fraction of the jobs classified by the company.

  • Write public summaries of non-capabilities R&D projects.

  • Check whether auditor-initiated workloads are classified correctly.

3.4 Review for warning signs. Are there major red flags?

  • Check for major contracts that subsidize inference for other large companies.

  • Check the distribution of non-capabilities compute. Is a single type of project absorbing huge amounts of compute?

  • Conduct private interviews with researchers to ask if they have observed anything suspicious.

After completing the audit, the auditor would write up a report containing:

  1. whether they agree with the AI company's disclosure and, if not, their independent estimate of compute usage.

  2. a description of their methodology.

  3. limitations of their audit, along with an estimate of total error (the capabilities-equivalent compute the audit could be missing, as a percentage of overall compute).

  4. a summary of N (e.g., 30) projects sampled from the non-capabilities bucket, weighted by compute use, with enough information to show an outside observer that each project was genuinely not capabilities work.

Attacks & Loopholes

If all we want is transparency, we think that baseline auditing would most likely be sufficient. However, if there is also a limit set on capabilities R&D compute — as we think there should be — then the stricter the limit, the greater the incentive to cheat. Baseline auditing would be insufficient to reliably verify pacing.

We think that if frontier AI companies were legally required to (i) disclose how they use their compute and (ii) use no more than X% on capabilities R&D, then the most likely outcome would be that all five leading U.S. companies comply. This is for the same reasons that they normally comply with laws — too many possible whistleblowers or other ways they could get caught. This is especially true since the point of noncompliance would be to get an advantage in AI R&D progress, but that advantage would be hard to hide — if your AI models leapfrog over those of your competitors, for example, that would raise suspicions. That being said, we think that cheating is a serious possibility, especially the kind where you do it in a plausibly deniable way so that if you get caught you don’t go straight to jail.

We lay out seven types of attack a malicious AI company could use to cheat the system, and describe two cheating scenarios — one in which they stick to plausibly deniable mechanisms (Scenario 1), and one in which there is deliberate deception by a leadership-backed conspiracy (Scenario 2). We lay out a baseline and a robust auditing proposal: baseline auditing is only effective against the first scenario, while robust auditing works against the second.

This table gives an estimate of the total error in each scenario. These are defined and justified in the Attacks and Loopholes supplement.

Scenario 1Plausibly deniableScenario 2Leadership-backed conspiracy
Baseline auditing7%55%
Robust auditing2%6%

In practice, we recommend that regulators implement regulation as soon as possible, with provisions that phase in progressively stronger auditing regimes, to get the incentives right. AI companies should know that soon there will be auditors checking for compliance, and that later there will be stronger, savvier auditors checking harder. This builds trust in the whole system and makes cheating much less likely to be attempted in the first place.

Robust Auditing

Robust auditing adds stronger measures to withstand significant adversarial pressure, such as:

  • KYC + auditing for major external users

  • AI R&D classifiers

  • Auditor-managed logging infrastructure

  • …

We believe that robust auditing is sufficient to keep error to ~6% of total compute, even assuming a leadership backed conspiracy.

We propose a set of additional measures that could improve on baseline auditing.

[Figure. With the additional measures proposed here, we could limit error to ~6%, assuming high-context auditors, even under Scenario 2 (leadership-backed conspiracy). Implementation pathways

There are several ways our proposal could be implemented and evolve over time. Some of the ways it can vary include the number of companies it applies to, whether it is voluntary or required by regulation, the level of granularity in disclosures, and the level of verification in place.

The pilot we propose is voluntary disclosures with third-party auditing. AI companies voluntarily disclose their compute allocations per our proposal and allow auditors to immediately carry out baseline auditing and then work up to robust auditing.

Why would companies voluntarily pace?

AI companies are in a collective action problem: they are proceeding faster than they believe optimal. VCAD supplies two elements that can help resolve the problem, prompting a race to the top.

  1. Trust: Claims of costly restraint today are not always believed by competitors. VCAD provides a way in which companies can take commercially costly actions in the interest of safety or security that competitors can trust.

  2. Public credit: VCAD’s public disclosures (the “D”) offer a simple, commensurable benchmark for cross-company comparisons, which can help channel public and policymaker concern into a concrete request: less compute on R&D.

Interest in pacing is high and will grow with evidence of risk. Demand for reduced R&D allocations gives companies a self-interested reason to reallocate and rewards those that do, spurring a race to the top. Each reallocation would be a unilateral response to, among other things, public demand based on a public benchmark. The dynamic does not depend on, and should not involve, agreement among companies on allocation levels.

There are two additional pathways that might be alternatives if the former fails (or that can be pursued in parallel) which we find promising, which vary in how much company and political will is required:

  • With less company will: voluntary binding disclosures without auditing. In this scenario, the companies could still voluntarily disclose their compute allocations via financial disclosures or Congress (where lying is a criminal offense), or via the SB 53 Frontier Safety Framework (where lying carries small civil penalties).[2]

  • With more political will: state or federal regulation. Domestic regulation, either state law or federal legislation passed by Congress, that applies to the top 5 AI companies or more, with verification through either more binding disclosures or, better, third-party or government auditing.

Implementation over time

1. Adoption

  • Voluntary — Companies voluntarily disclose their compute allocations and use them to credibly demonstrate pacing.

  • Domestic regulation — State or federal. Options include: (i) just disclosure + verification; (ii) disclosure + verification + empowering an agency to mandate reallocations; (iii) a component of a conditional regime (see 4 below).

  • Long term: International regulation

These steps can happen in sequence; alternatively, the voluntary regime can be skipped or cut short by domestic regulation.

2. Coverage

  • US Top 2 (e.g., OpenAI and Anthropic) — These companies have a ~3-month lead over everyone else.

  • US Top 5 (OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, GDM, xAI) — These companies have a ~6-month lead over everyone else.

  • All domestic US AI companies

  • Long term: International — Eventually, AI regulation that would prevent the development of misaligned superintelligence needs to be international, including in China.

3. Disclosure granularity

We think the categories of compute per our diagram in this proposal, together with some transparency on the workloads that get classified as non-capabilities, should be the baseline for what all companies do in common.

  • Our initial diagram + Safety Transparency — Report compute allocations for each of: capabilities R&D, non-capabilities R&D, serving customers, classifiers, and idle compute. For non-capabilities R&D, take a representative sample of that compute and publish a summary.

  • Granular reporting — Everything above, plus more granular categories, such as a breakdown of inference into RL rollouts/synthetic data, autonomous agent swarms, model evaluations, and employee use.

  • Long term: Total Research Transparency — As much as possible is public; auditors on the inside work to ensure that nearly all risk-relevant information is public, including compute allocations.

4. Combination with safety and security requirements

We don’t currently have a science of AI risk sufficient to make conditional triggers that will be robust in the future, so we think an unconditional implementation of this proposal is needed as a stopgap.

  • Unconditional — Set a capabilities compute cap unconditionally, and adjust it over time as needed without explicit triggers.

  • Long term: Conditional — A component of a mature governance regime, with safety and security requirements as triggers.

5. Verification

To be effective, disclosures must be trusted within a reasonable margin of error (e.g., <5% of total compute). The burden of verification will increase with how strong the incentives are to misreport and which actors are involved.

  • No external verification: SB 53 FSF — Part of the framework that AI companies are required to follow under California’s SB 53. Violation incurs a small fine (<=$1M).

  • Ongoing financial disclosures — Deception exposes the company to investor lawsuits and exposes executives to criminal liability.

  • External verification: Third-party embedded baseline audit — Third-party auditor gets employee-level access, allowing them to directly inspect logging infrastructure, submit jobs, and red-team the classifiers.

  • Third-party robust audit — The third party can do everything in our Robust Auditing section.

  • Long term: Hardware Verification — Robust hardware security properties, paired with well-developed software measures such as ZKPs, etc.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why pace?

  1. Timelines to recursive self-improvement (RSI) are most likely short. Our best guess is that, absent a deliberate slowdown, AIs will fully automate the process of AI R&D before EOY 2027.

  2. We aren’t anywhere near ready to do full RSI. This is true for many reasons.

    • Loss of control: Current AIs are misaligned. Continuing to improve capabilities without substantial improvements to alignment would pose a large risk of AI takeover. Even if we think current AIs are safe, recursive self-improvement will increase the pace of AI progress and reduce human understanding, so misalignment will probably get worse. We will probably need to slow down during the intelligence explosion, so we need to establish the mechanism to do so as soon as possible.

    • Concentration of power: Even if AI companies manage to align their “army of geniuses in the datacenters”, that would be an unacceptable concentration of power. A tiny group of CEOs or politicians could end up choosing the values of the army of geniuses which obsolete humanity. AI-powered oligarchy or dictatorship are live possibilities.

    • Misuse risk: Bioweapons are extremely hard to defend against. The cost and expertise needed to make an engineered pathogen are decreasing rapidly. Resilience and defense are not keeping pace.

  3. Pacing would delay RSI. It would give us more time for:

    • Alignment and control R&D.

    • The public and governments to wake up and learn about what’s going on.

    • Legislation to be crafted, voted on, and implemented.

How much would compute reallocation slow things down?

This depends on what the capabilities R&D dial is set to, how much error there is in the regime, and what the production function for AI progress is with respect to R&D compute. If we assume the capabilities allocation is set to 20% and 6% error is exploited, then the resulting 26% allocation would be an immediate ~3x reduction in capabilities R&D compute for Anthropic (which uses an estimated ~75% of its compute on capabilities R&D today).

We don’t know how much overall AI progress would slow down due to an ongoing 3x reduction in R&D compute, because there are other inputs to AI progress and we don’t know how important each of them is. However, our best guess is that it would slow progress down by around 1.5-2x[3] in the short term. Over time, the pace of progress is determined by the growth rate of compute, so assuming the company’s compute buildout is similar under pacing, its speed would converge back to the previous rate.

Imagine a phantom copy of the company that has 3x less compute, growing at the same rate. This phantom company would follow behind the leader with a fixed calendar time delay, but move at the same pace (because it has as much compute as the frontier company had a fixed time ago).[4] The one-time 3x reduction in compute puts the frontier company in the phantom company’s position from that point onward, so its progress converges towards the phantom company’s trajectory.

[Figure: AI Futures Model with constant compute growth and a later takeoff. A 3x cut in capabilities compute from January 2027 delays SAR by about 7 months and TED-AI by about 8 months; the paced path converges to the path of a company that always had 3x less compute. capability · 2027 · 2028 · 2029 · 2030 · SAR · +7 mo · TED-AI · +8 mo · pacing starts · No pacing · Pacing: 3x less capabilities compute · Always had 3x less compute]

AI Futures Model with constant compute growth and a later takeoff (different from runs in table below)

As a result, later capability milestones are delayed more (the delay is still growing towards the fixed calendar lag), but the slowdown in the rate at which milestones are crossed shrinks towards zero. So the compute reduction mainly pushes back timelines, and its effect on the speed of takeoff is smaller the further away takeoff is. This assumes compute growth is constant; if compute growth slows in the future (as is likely, absent large AI-driven speedups), then takeoff could also be slower. In practice, though, timelines to highly capable AI might be short enough that this convergence doesn’t have time to matter much.

In a run of our AI Futures Model (which, without pacing, reaches Superhuman AI Researcher (SAR) in August 2027 and Top-Expert-Dominating-AI (TED-AI) in October 2027), a 3x cut from January 2027 delays SAR by about 4 months and TED-AI by about 5 months, and the paced company crosses both about 24% slower than it would without pacing.

What about China?

The US should care about both the absolute level of risk from continued AI development and its relative lead over China. Even if you care only about the relative lead over China and don’t believe in the risks, the downsides of this proposal are likely much smaller than you might expect. This rests on the following core arguments:

  1. Security is poor enough such that China could catch up to the US at any time anyway.

    AI companies are not on track to be secure against efforts by China to steal their IP (OC4 or OC5 efforts as defined by RAND). Therefore, assuming China decides to put effort into stealing from US AI companies, there is not much upside to continuing to develop new algorithmic secrets and models.

  2. Slowing down may make it possible to improve security without giving China the opportunity to steal higher-risk IP in the meantime.

    Improving security could make it harder for China to steal AIs and training recipes at the US frontier. It might be possible to make significant security improvements for model weights, dataset and distillation (and potentially on code and algorithm confidentiality) that enable the US to maintain a more robust lead in the future. The tractability of doing so is uncertain, especially for algorithm confidentiality, but at the very least a slowdown would mean that China can steal less capable models than it otherwise would.

  3. Slowing down buys more time to possibly reach an agreement with China.

    By slowing down, the US can signal seriousness about the risks of further AI development, and negotiate an agreement with China for both countries to proceed with sufficient caution, in a commensurable and verifiable way.

[Figure: Sketches of US and China progress under each scenario. 1. The US lead is · vulnerable to China · stealing · US · China steals · China · 2. Slowing down can make · stealing less likely and · less bad · US · China steals · China · 3. Slowing down can let · us make an international · agreement · US · China]

  1. The US has a large compute advantage over China, so in worlds where China does not aggressively steal from the US, the US labs could carry out significant pacing while still maintaining a lead.

    In worlds where China isn’t aggressively stealing progress from the US, the US could adopt a ‘China-dominating’ pacing proposal in which US companies in aggregate still have more compute going to capabilities R&D than China (e.g., if the gap over Chinese companies is ~10x, a 20% compute cap still leaves US companies with at least twice as much capabilities R&D compute). This would allow the US to pace while still maintaining a lead. If China aggressively steals US progress, it would become much less clear if this strategy is sufficient to maintain a lead.

This proposal would be net negative only if both of the following are true:

  1. The risks from continued AI development are low in the near future.

  2. China is unlikely to put much effort into stealing US progress in the near future.

If these are both true, then the US would be giving up some of its lead for little gain. If only (1) is true, then the US isn’t really giving up its lead through this proposal (China would have caught up regardless via theft), and if only (2) is true, then spending some of the US lead was worth it because it reduced risk.

Why not a different mechanism for pacing?

We can think of the options for slowing down AI progress by looking at the set of inputs to AI progress, which are R&D compute and labor, where R&D compute can be used on experiments, training runs and AI automation.

[Figure: Inputs to AI progress and where each pacing option limits them: human labor and R&D compute; R&D compute is used for automated researchers, experiments and training; compute reallocation, researcher holidays and an internal deployment lag limit inputs to algorithmic progress; capabilities limitations limit training only. INPUTS · USES OF R&D COMPUTE · R&D compute · Human labor · Training · Experiments · Automated · researchers · Algorithmic · progress · AI · capabilities · Compute reallocation · Researcher holidays · Internal deployment lag · Capabilities limitations]

Each of these inputs could be limited in quantity (e.g., a cap on compute spend) or regulated by safety standards (e.g., banning training runs that use neuralese algorithms). The decision to restrict inputs or require safeguards could be part of a pacing regime that is triggered by reaching a pre-registered risk level (e.g., safety-case-based pacing), reaching a pre-registered capability level (e.g., RSPs), or one that has no pre-registered triggers.

Writing good safety standards that sufficiently address the sources of risk will require a lot of institutional capacity, increased scientific understanding, and ongoing iteration, so this approach cannot be deployed quickly as a pacing measure.

Therefore, limiting inputs to AI progress is the more promising near-term pacing solution. However, limits that directly gate AI capabilities (without also gating algorithmic progress) could create an algorithmic overhang.

[Figure: Two panels. No Pacing: the models trained follow the rising curve of what could be trained. Temporary Capabilities Cap: trained models stay flat from the start of the cap to its end, then rise in one step to the curve, which is somewhat lower than without the cap. No Pacing · capability · time · can train · Temporary Capabilities Cap · capability · time · cap starts · cap ends · no pacing · can train]

If we slow down via anything but limiting algorithmic progress, this creates an algorithmic overhang, which, once training resumes, results in a rapid return to something similar to the original trend (though it’s somewhat lower due to reduced AI R&D uplift). This algorithmic overhang could, in principle, become very large. Algorithmic progress is fast and is likely to accelerate in the future: estimates of algorithmic progress today range from 3x to 30x per year, and it seems plausible that algorithmic progress recently has been even faster. Because algorithmic progress is more rapid than compute progress (which is ~5x/yr), and all of the built-up progress could be immediately applied to a new training run while applying a compute overhang would be intermediated by R&D, an algorithmic overhang could be much worse than a compute overhang.

The algorithmic overhang creates two major problems:

  • Discontinuous rapid progress. If the capabilities cap is temporary, then lifting it would cause a discontinuous jump in capabilities, which could be very dangerous.

  • Poor AI company security means that the unused algorithms still accelerate trailing actors. AI companies are not robust to algorithmic leakage. It is likely that any algorithmic progress made, even if it isn't used in a final training run at the compliant AI company, could get used by other AI projects.

In an emergency situation, which we may soon find ourselves in, direct AI capability restrictions may be necessary. However, we’d recommend pairing these with measures to limit algorithmic progress, in order to prevent an algorithmic progress overhang.

There are several options for limiting algorithmic progress that we think are promising, including:

  1. Compute allocation caps to R&D. This is the proposal we analyzed in this post.

  2. Creating a lag in the internal deployment of AI models. This could involve creating a delay between the time that a new model is trained and when it is allowed to be deployed internally. We discuss the implementation of the deployment lag proposal in more detail here.

  3. Researcher holidays. This could involve AI researchers only working one or two days a week, with all their associated work (e.g., experiments) also stopping on the days they don’t work.

We specifically analyzed the compute allocation cap in this post, but a similar verification methodology would be required for the other measures for limiting algorithmic progress inputs. This is because the problem will continue to have the structure where:

  1. The company has compute that it could use for R&D but is not supposed to (up to some limit, for some categories of uses).

  2. The company could have access to other sources of compute that it can use freely.

[1] We’re especially interested in a low false-negative rate, i.e., that the capabilities classifier doesn’t miss substantial fractions of the capabilities research.

[2] There would still be a risk of plausibly deniable deception (or willful deception) from AI companies, but the scope of declarations could be expanded to try and reduce this surface area. We are unsure how much error there would be in this scenario, but it seems plausible that it would galvanize enough self-verification for <5% error, because the CEO and board may want to be really sure they aren’t lying in these disclosures.

[3] Assuming a simple model of AI progress (Cobb-Douglas in compute and labor: C^α · L^(1−α)). With a compute share α of 0.4–0.6, a 3x cut gives 3^α ≈ 1.55x–1.9x; α = 0.5 gives 1.73x. The bounds are 1x (compute doesn’t matter) and 3x (compute is the only bottleneck). The truth seems very likely to be somewhere in the middle.

[4] Assuming they also have 3x less of all other inputs to AI progress.

[5] The AI Futures Model (November 2026 code) with Daniel Kokotajlo’s August 2026 median parameters and these parameter changes: serial coding uplift 7x in August 2026 (preset 2x); excess uplift doubling time 3.5 months (preset 5); coding labor substitutability ρ = −0.2 (preset −2); experiment capacity ceiling from infinite coding labor 60x (preset 15x); slowdown from 10x less experiment compute 1.5x (preset 2.8x); AI research taste slope 2.3 SD per 2025-progress-year (preset 3.0); AI research taste at −1.5 SD on November 1, 2026. Trajectory without pacing.

[6] The AI Futures Model (same code) with Eli Lifland’s August 2026 median parameters and these parameter changes: serial coding uplift 12x in October 2026 (preset 1.7x); excess uplift doubling time 3.5 months (preset 6.5), chosen so that SAR without pacing matches the modified run. Trajectory without pacing.

Baseline methodology

Baseline Methodology

We propose a methodology with the following properties:

  • It could be implemented today (it does not rely on new science).
  • It is not sufficient to withstand adversarial pressure from a company trying to actively lie in their disclosure, which could happen under a pacing regime where companies are supposed to significantly limit compute used for capabilities.

We believe this methodology is sufficient to give an accurate estimate of current AI company compute allocations, assuming little adversarial pressure—for example, in the situation where it's just a transparency regime, and so AI companies have little incentive to deceive about their compute allocations.

Each company should create a database that accounts for all the compute (measured in GPU-hours) that the company uses (more detail on the scope here). Each entry in the table should have the GPU-hours used by the workload, and depending on which of the following categories of workload it fits into, it should have the following metadata attached to the log:

Workload TypeUserGPU TypeTime windowModelDataTranscriptFeeds into training?Other
R&DOwner✓✓Code & DatasetsPointers to (i) workloads & agents started by this process and (ii) the agent that started the job
External inferenceAPI Key / OAuth✓✓✓Tokens✓ iff not ZDR✓
Internal inferenceAPI Key✓✓✓Tokens✓ iff not ZDR✓Pointer to AI R&D jobs launched
MonitoringOwner✓✓✓Tokens✓ iff input not ZDRPointer to workloads it's monitoring

Step 2 involves three substages: 2.1) Aggregate GPU-hours. 2.2) Classify workloads into capabilities vs. non-capabilities. 2.3) Estimate idle compute.

2.1) Aggregate GPU-hours. Getting an overall estimate of compute use requires aggregating across heterogeneous GPUs into a single unified GPU-hr metric (e.g., “H100-equivalents”). We discuss this in more detail in an appendix.

2.2) Classify workloads into capabilities vs. non-capabilities, using a mixture of AI classification and manual human classification. By “capabilities” compute, we mean compute that has any positive capabilities effects — including work that has capabilities and safety externalities. This centrally includes:

  • Experiments to improve algorithms and data
  • Data generation or filtering
  • Training more capable AIs
  • Internal inference in service of the above

Unfortunately, it’s hard to give a crisp definition of this, and there are many edge cases. The exact definition isn’t that important so long as it isn’t possible to use internal non-capabilities compute in a way that has large capabilities externalities. We discuss this in more detail in a supplement here.

2.3) Estimate idle compute. By idle compute, we mean compute that is not turned on or is not in use. This includes:

  • Hot spares
  • Downtime
  • New racks that haven’t started use

When Step 2 is complete, the company will have an internal estimate of compute allocation such as the following:

The categories are defined as follows:

  • Serving customers: compute used to serve customers, including via API, web interfaces (e.g., Claude.ai), and desktop (e.g., Claude Code). We also call this category “External Inference”.
    • The “trained on” box is the subset of external inference that feeds back into capabilities, either by being directly trained on, paraphrased and then trained on, or similar.
  • Safeguard classifiers: monitors checking for misuse
  • Internal Inference: inference compute used for internal AI company use. This includes evaluations, internal coding agents, and RL rollouts.
    • We subdivide internal inference into capabilities and safety, where safety compute refers to the internal inference that doesn’t have significant capabilities externalities.
  • Non-Capabilities R&D: R&D compute that has minimal capabilities externalities.
  • Capabilities R&D: all other R&D compute.

See Supplement C for more detail on the definitions.

The AI company publishes a disclosure of the compute allocation. We could imagine, for example, a disclosure every two weeks covering compute allocation over that period. This report should include:

  • An overall estimate of compute allocation
  • An overview of the methodology used to make and audit that estimate
  • An analysis of possible mistakes, discrepancies the auditor was not able to resolve, and an estimate of the error rate
  • Chip-conversion ratios
  • Descriptions of N (e.g., 30) non-capabilities projects, randomly sampled in proportion to compute

We recommend that AI companies publish this disclosure through a channel that punishes misreporting. As a starting point, it should be part of the company’s SB 53 frontier AI framework. As soon as possible, it should move to a channel with real liability, such as being included in financial disclosures or directly required by regulation with sufficient teeth to deter violation.

Even with improved reporting channels, there would still be risk of:

  • Deception from AI executives
  • Goodharting: for the attacks we’re most worried about, it can happen without explicit deception, particularly attack 5 (external compute) and attack 7 (misclassifying capabilities compute). We’d recommend these reports explicitly make claims about the company not doing activities in these buckets.
  • Internal conspiracies the leadership doesn’t know about.

Despite this, such a requirement would probably galvanize a lot of self-verification internally, because the CEO and board may want to be really sure they aren’t lying in these disclosures.

A third-party auditor verifies the disclosure. This will involve auditing (and potentially reproducing parts of) the accounting process that was previously done by the company. The baseline verification process involves the following substages:

3.1) Completeness: does the table include all the compute?

  • The auditors review financial data to make sure that the total GPU-hrs being reported by the company match the amount of compute it should have, given its compute contracts.
  • Datacenter capacity information

3.2) Integrity: is the information in the table a correct accounting of workloads in the company?

  • Spot-check a random set of workloads to confirm that the metadata is consistent with the reported GPU-hrs, by estimating the compute requirements from the auditors’ best understanding of the stack. Optionally, this could be assisted by increased visibility into the compilers and performance of the live stack on different workloads.
  • Directly review the logging code to check for bugs and/or backdoors

3.3) Classification accuracy

  • Run an independent classification pipeline
  • Manually review a fraction of the jobs classified by the company
  • Write public summaries of non-capabilities R&D projects.

3.4) Look for signs of goodharting with substantial fractions of compute

  • Are there major contracts that subsidize inference for other large companies.
  • Is a particular non-capabilities project absorbing huge amounts of compute?

The auditors can additionally conduct private interviews with researchers, to ask if they have observed anything suspicious, and to randomly check if workloads they initiated have been logged correctly.

Supplement A · Attacks & Loopholes

Attacks & Loopholes

Using the baseline methodology to verify a cap on capabilities compute would be open to many attacks. In this supplement we give a taxonomy of these attacks and estimate how much capabilities compute each could unlock under two concrete scenarios.

We express each estimate as capabilities-equivalent compute: the share of the company’s total compute that, if simply added to the capped allocation, would help capabilities R&D as much as the attack does. Compute gained through an attack is usually less useful than ordinary capabilities compute, so an attack that diverts 6% of total compute at a 3x penalty counts as 2%. We call this the error of the auditing.1We’ll assume that pacing is implemented via a capabilities compute cap of 20%, and so our errors are measured relative to increasing compute beyond a default margin of 20%.

However:

  • This is just one possible choice of cap — it may become important to dial the compute cap down more aggressively.
  • There are other viable proposals for pacing (such as internal deployment lags) that rely on similar mechanisms.

Our bottom line takeaway is that the baseline methodology is insufficient to verify this capabilities compute ceiling.

In Robust Auditing, we propose improvements to the methodology and analyze how this more intensive auditing regime would fare at verifying a compute cap under the same two concrete scenarios.

A taxonomy of attacks on the baseline auditing regime

We identify 7 classes of attacks that AI companies could use to increase their capabilities compute usage without being visible to the auditors, and we estimate how much error each attack could cause under the baseline auditing methodology.

Another loophole not pictured here is to increase compute faster than you otherwise would have: e.g., AI companies could acquire cloud compute providers. A percentage cap, which only applies to frontier AI companies, will necessarily create distorted incentives like this; to avoid incentives like this, you need absolute caps or a cap-and-trade system. However, we’re not very worried about this attack because:

  • AI companies are already a large fraction of the world’s compute. There isn’t that much more room for them to grow.
  • This attack is extremely expensive. This makes it slow and transparent, enabling a response from other parties.
  • Structurally, this loophole moves more of the world’s compute into the “paced” fraction.

Summary of the attacks

  1. Hidden compute. The company uses off-books compute that auditors don’t know about. This can be used arbitrarily, but it might be hard to discreetly access internal model weights and datasets.
  2. Fake idle compute. The company uses GPU-hours that it reports to the auditors as idle. For example, chips that are supposed to be ‘hot spares’ (lying dormant alongside a training workload for redundancy in case of failures) or chips that typically sit unused (e.g., experiment compute or inference chips during off hours, like overnight).
  3. Hidden efficiency. The company uses GPU-hours differently from what it declares, either by doing the declared workload more efficiently than what the auditors believe or by not doing the declared workload and doing something cheaper instead.
  4. Launder internal inference. The company makes internal inference appear to be external inference, by giving employees external API keys, and potentially giving these keys special permissions or access (e.g., unreleased models, classifiers off). If it can disable any classifiers, it can use this for R&D; otherwise the company could use it to generate synthetic training data that doesn’t trigger the classifiers.
  5. Use external inference for R&D or training data via collaborating third parties. The company could reach explicit or implicit agreements to have external inference compute used for capabilities benefit, with third-party actors doing R&D directly or generating training data while evading R&D classifiers. (We don't yet have a specific proposal for exactly what the R&D classifiers should count as in vs. out; more work here would be very useful. It will involve some difficult decisions, such as where to draw the line between video game coding and RL environment generation. Auditors could also monitor for spikes in a particular class of external inference.)
  6. Use normal external inference as training data. The company directly uses real data from normal external inference traffic as training material to improve model capabilities.
  7. Exploit the capabilities vs. non-capabilities classification. The company subverts the capabilities vs. non-capabilities classifier explicitly (e.g., by jailbreaking it) or finds edge cases to goodhart the classifier and get as much capabilities benefit as possible.

For each attack, we will cover the core steps involved in carrying out the attack, the personnel needed to carry out the attack or required to have knowledge of the attack, and quantitatively how much compute the attack might unlock (and what type of compute) under two concrete scenarios explained below.

Two scenarios we consider:

The amount of compute that an attack can unlock will depend on how far the company is willing to go to subvert the regime. One way to think about it is in terms of what tier of violation from the taxonomy below it falls into, and how many people carrying out each kind of violation (or having knowledge thereof) would be required:

  1. Goodharting metrics (e.g., the capabilities vs. non-capabilities classifier, or using external contractors)
  2. Actively lying (e.g., misreporting idle GPUs, claiming they aren’t aware of any subversions, hiding efficiencies)
  3. Egregious deception (e.g., hacking the logging code, lying to many employees)
  4. Committing crimes (e.g., financial fraud to rent off-books compute, breaking ZDR contracts)

We define two scenarios that seem most important to think about: the first because it seems the most likely for a voluntary agreement, and the second because it seems important for how companies might model each other.

Scenario 1: Plausibly deniable. The company will break the spirit of the declaration (e.g., use non-capabilities compute for capabilities research, and contract external actors for capabilities benefits) but will not lie to auditors, backdoor its own infrastructure, or commit crimes. However, a small group (e.g., 1-3) of rogue employees may unilaterally attempt egregious deception without leadership knowledge or with tacit leadership approval.

Scenario 2: Leadership-backed conspiracy. Leadership is willing to lie to auditors and instruct employees to tamper with logging infrastructure. We assume that the conspiracy can consist of no more than ~30 people (due to risk of whistleblowing).

Attack 1: Hidden compute

This attack requires buying or renting compute without leaving a paper trail that financial auditing could identify as a compute-related transaction.

Attack steps required:

  1. Funding source. To buy or rent compute, the company needs a funding source. There are several ways it might get one, but the most promising seems to be large shareholders (e.g., founders or long-time employees) selling shares in the company, which should become easy if the company IPOs. Anthropic's Q3 compute spend was $10B and its valuation is ~$2T, a 200x multiple. This means that 0.5% of the shares would be enough to match their entire quarterly compute spend. (This ratio is probably similar at OpenAI.) Another method might be to falsify or inflate contracts (e.g., bonuses to employees or contracts for buying data) and have a secret agreement to deliver compute as part of this, though this seems easier to trace via financial auditing.
  1. Compute source. Once funding is in a bank account that is not visible to the auditors (e.g., the personal bank account of an employee or an offshore shell company), they could rent compute on the open market, however, the depth of market here might be shallow. For above $1B of compute per quarter it may require buying out a startup’s (e.g., Thinking Machines’) entire contract or multiple small neoclouds’ entire clusters. Another possibility might be to rent compute from clusters that have been set up by chip smugglers (e.g., shell companies in Malaysia). To the extent these clusters exist, they might be the best option, because they might accept harder-to-track forms of payment (e.g., crypto). Another option is to set up a new datacenter from scratch, securing orders for compute, but the lead time on this is probably at least 12 months (maybe less if you buy out a project that was close to having compute online).

Personnel requirements:

  1. Conspirators for funding. Plausibly, funding for this attack at a ~10% of company compute ($1B/quarter) scale can be concentrated in 1-3 large individual shareholders, or 1-3 average employees at a ~1% of company compute ($100M/quarter) scale.
  2. Conspirators for compute. The same 1-3 large individual shareholders can plausibly figure out a hard-to-track compute source. This would probably require paying around 1.5-2x above market price, and seems difficult to push far above ~$1B of compute (around 10% of frontier company compute) without being among the largest compute-related transactions.
  3. Employees to use the compute. Using ~10% of the company’s compute effectively will probably require around 10 researchers. It seems very difficult to set up the compute in a way that these researchers wouldn’t know they are using external compute, and random interviews might reveal the lack of logging, so these 10 researchers would have to be complicit in the scheme. This number might be much lower as research becomes increasingly automated (e.g., could be 0 at full AI R&D automation).

Estimates of the quantity of compute achievable with this attack in the first 6 months.

Scenario 1: Plausibly deniable. With only 1-3 disgruntled employees attempting this (excluding leadership), they are probably constrained by funding unless they happen to have a top-10 early employee among them. We might expect the average group to have around 0.04% of equity, and assuming they are willing to sell down 40% of this per quarter, they’d be selling 0.016% of equity, which is enough to match 3.2% of the company’s quarterly compute spend (at a 200x equity to quarterly compute spend ratio). Assuming a ~1.5x overhead to secure the compute at this scale, this is equivalent to ~2% of the company’s compute. In this scenario, it seems unlikely that the tiny conspiracy would be able to smuggle out frontier internal model weights or datasets, so this compute would probably be significantly less useful than internal compute. We apply a 2x discount for this (it’s probably easy enough to funge with other internal uses at this small scale).

Scenario 2: Leadership-backed conspiracy. With a broader conspiracy, funding is no longer the constraint, and the amount of compute that can be secured via hard-to-trace channels becomes binding. This seems to be around 20% of the company’s compute spend at a 2x overhead on average. The biggest uncertainty here is around the availability of grey-market compute rental or buy-outs from smuggled GPU markets, and how easy it would be to make large US-based neocloud or startup buyouts without appearing to be linked to the AI company. Under this wider conspiracy, it seems possible for the company to share sufficient model weights or datasets with the external compute to make it fungible with internal capabilities compute.

Attack 1: Hidden compute
Scenario 1: plausibly deniable1%
Scenario 2: leadership-backed conspiracy10%

Attack 2: Fake idle compute

This attack requires making use of compute that would be idle by default, which might include entire servers that happen not to have jobs scheduled at some times, or GPUs that are purposefully left idle as part of a larger workload (e.g., ‘hot spares’ for redundancy in training run workloads).

Attack steps required:

  1. Disable the logging on otherwise-idle compute. This attack requires a way of assigning workloads to idle GPUs without the rest of the company noticing, and without any automated logging systems detecting these workloads. Depending on how well the companies implement logging systems, it might be very easy to do this, or it might require hacking the logging infrastructure, which may be increasingly difficult without certain levels of security access.

Personnel requirements:

  1. Disabling the logging infrastructure. It might require 1-3 employees with special security permissions and AI assistance to disable the logging infrastructure selectively in cases where it is being used by the co-conspiring employees.
  2. Employees to use the compute. Again, employees using the idle compute will likely have to be complicit, because it will be easy for them to notice their workloads not getting logged. To use ~10% of company compute effectively, you would probably need a 10-person team.

Estimates of the quantity of compute achievable with this attack in the first 6 months.

Scenario 1: Plausibly deniable. In the near term, internal security at companies is probably not sufficient to prevent a typical tiny conspiracy of internal employees from implementing a vulnerability in the logging infrastructure to make use of idle compute. However, pulling off workloads on ‘hot spares’ seems more difficult, given the need to manage potential conflicts with another legitimate workload, so the most promising approach seems to be to opportunistically run workloads whenever the rest of the company happens to leave capacity idle (e.g., overnight, when idle compute may be especially high). Our guess is that around 3% of the compute will be usable in this type of way. The biggest uncertainties here are what percentage of company compute is typically completely idle by default, and how difficult it would be to disable the logging measures.

Scenario 2: Leadership-backed conspiracy. With a broader conspiracy, it should not only be easy to subvert the logging systems to use idle compute untracked, but it’s also probably possible to inflate the pool of idle GPUs by slightly sandbagging on various related optimizations, e.g., overprovisioning ‘hot spares’ on workloads, not trying maximally hard to utilize compute overnight. SemiAnalysis reports that Nvidia recommends at least one compute tray per NVL rack as a hot spare (idle GPUs ready to pick up on failed workloads), and claims the NVL72’s 72-GPUs are 64 active and 8 standby (about 11%) for training workloads. Our guess is that the average ‘hot spares’ ratio across all workloads might be around 6% and can be sandbagged to average around 10%, with the difference being easy to use freely with slack on interconnect bandwidth (this is probably less useful than entirely free clusters because it is more spread out, but it can probably be made fungible at this scale by using it for small workloads). Another ~4% of compute can probably be used opportunistically when entire clusters happen to be idle (e.g., overnight).

Attack 2: Fake idle compute
Scenario 1: plausibly deniable3%
Scenario 2: leadership-backed conspiracy8%

Attack 3: Hidden efficiency

This attack involves overreporting the compute usage of uncapped (non-capabilities) workloads, and then using the spare compute for capabilities work that doesn’t count towards the cap.

Attack steps required:

  1. Overreport compute used by uncapped workloads. There are several different approaches that could be used here, including:
    1. Entirely faking workloads and metadata which never actually run and adding them to the logging tables.
    2. Falsifying some isolated part of the reporting of a real workload, e.g., what model is running or how many CoT tokens were generated.
    3. Accurately reporting a workload, but running it more efficiently (with fewer GPU-hrs, or leaving spare GPU capacity) than the logging shows.
    4. (Goodharting-only variation) Forgoing runtime efficiency optimizations on uncapped workloads to focus on making more optimizations on the capped workloads.

    For some versions of these attacks, it might be possible to fool the logging systems into overreporting the workloads in isolated ways, without any elevated control over the logging systems. For example, the logging system could be reading and logging the true workload correctly, except for some small portion of the code and some faked telemetry readings.

    Targeting the largest single workloads seems like the most promising version of this attack. If you can find a way for large portions of production inference (e.g., all ZDR inference from a certain model or cluster) to be systematically overreported, this might free up a very large percentage of the compute in a predictable way, that could be optimized to be used in parallel with the reported workload without conflicting over the hardware resources.

  2. Evading the logging on the spare compute. Once uncapped uses of the compute have been overreported, the company can use this overreported compute for capped use cases (capabilities). This may still require disabling any automated logging systems that might report metadata about these hidden workloads to the auditors. For versions of the attack that fall under point C above, i.e., running the true workload but with a different lower-level implementation and a hidden workload in parallel, this step may not be required at all (e.g., if the code for hidden compute use is injected at some lower layer that is not observable to the logging systems). Note that depending on the form of overreporting, the spare compute may be in the form of entirely idle servers, or might be in spare resource capacity alongside another ongoing workload.

Personnel requirements:

  1. Overreporting uncapped compute. How many people need to be involved will depend on how many have access to information that would reveal the overreporting, and how much manual work it requires.
    1. Some versions of this attack involve implementing low-level efficiencies. It seems plausible that a relatively small set of people (e.g., 5-10 people) might be involved in the low-level optimizations related to large parts of the production inference traffic. Targeted actions from this group of people to tweak small things about the stack (e.g., parallelism choices, sandbagging on the true performance of runtime optimizations, speculative decoding params, routing behavior, etc.) might have significant efficiency effects on large parts of production inference traffic (e.g., perhaps 20-30% swings) without this being very noticeable to anyone else.
    2. Versions of this attack that involve falsifying logs. Apart from the teams that are in charge of optimizing these workloads with a large compute footprint, typical research teams probably shouldn’t bother trying to optimize workloads, and should just directly fabricate a bunch of fake logging entries in an automated way, by hacking or tricking the logging systems. If they aim to overreport their own workloads, this approach can only scale up to the team’s compute budget though, and they would need to have approval or a lot of freedom from the hierarchy above them to get away with not doing the type of research they are supposed to be doing. A better strategy is probably to generate fake external inference traffic. The most promising way to do this might be to inflate the usage of existing subscribers (no additional paper trail, e.g., overreporting the CoT tokens used in their traffic). An effective conspiracy here therefore seems like it requires some people responsible for production inference offerings, with the necessary access to do an overreporting hack.
  2. Disabling logging for hidden compute. The actions taken by the teams to overreport logging of the uncapped workloads, in terms of partial or full control over the logging system (or just what it observes), seem sufficient to also ensure the additional hidden compute usage is not reported for cases where that is necessary.
  3. Using the hidden compute. The people involved in overreporting the uncapped compute usage could also be the ones using the freed-up hidden compute if they are a research team falsifying logs. But if they are a team that works on optimizing the stack (e.g., production inference), they might not have the skills of AI capabilities researchers, so you might need a separate team of researchers to use the compute freed up by the hidden efficiency.

Estimates of the quantity of compute achievable with this attack in the first 6 months.

Scenario 1: Plausibly deniable. The goodharting-only version of this attack would be to disinvest time and resources from optimizing the runtime of all uncapped workloads (e.g., move people optimizing the production inference stack to optimizing the capped capabilities workloads). This would not free up compute like the full versions of this attack, but it would mean that capped workloads are generally more effective at using GPU-time compared to the worlds without the compute allocation cap. This effect seems like it could be substantial, and increasing over time. Our best guess is that over 6 months it could make the capped 20% capabilities compute 1.1x better utilized on average, comparable to ~22% of compute in the default world, where effort on optimizing inference and R&D workloads was allocated more evenly. There is a lot of uncertainty here about how much more companies will value the capped capabilities compute compared to the inference compute, which will determine the ratio of how much more they care about optimizing it, and details about optimizations (how broad the ongoing room for improvement is, how steep the diminishing returns are, and what resources it requires, e.g., possibly it will be highly automated and cheap to do everywhere). A tiny conspiracy seems like it would have a hard time adding much to this simple goodharting. The main option seems to be inflating the compute usage of their own workloads, but doing so egregiously would be noticeable to managers (e.g., completely doing other workloads instead) and they are unlikely to be lucky enough to be overseeing implementation details of large parts of compute usage (e.g., parts of the production inference stack). Assuming a random 1-3 employee conspiracy has around 0.2% of the company’s compute allocation, it seems difficult for them to sandbag more than a 2x overhead on what they are supposed to use the compute for, so they could free up about 0.1% of compute. This also assumes the logging systems aren’t robust enough to stop them from gaining the necessary control over what gets reported about their workloads.

Scenario 2: Leadership-backed conspiracy. A larger conspiracy seems like it could involve a team of around 10 people that work on part of the production inference stack, 10 capabilities researchers to use the compute, and extra people in the hierarchy that are in on this scheme and keep it hidden. We assume inference is 65% of reported compute allocation after the 20% cap. Probably the 10-person team can get away with implementing a 20% hidden efficiency on the production inference stack on average over 6 months (starting from lower), mostly by sandbagging slightly relative to known internal techniques (especially initially) and then building up more novel techniques over time while keeping them secret. This would free up around 13% of total compute. This same capabilities team can probably squeeze out more compute by inflating or fabricating external inference traffic from existing customers, especially ZDR customers, particularly by overreporting the lengths or models used in CoT generation or summarization pipelines, or potentially misreporting model routing that happens under the hood in inference offerings. Doing so within usage limits of subscriber based models seems like the most promising, because it involves no faked financial transactions. This could cause additional overreporting of around 10% of inference traffic on average over 6 months (starting lower and rising over time).

Another method would be to take capabilities researchers and have them directly fabricate or inflate the reporting on the non-capabilities workloads they are supposed to be doing, but this seems very hard to do at any significant scale (e.g., above 2% of compute) without being a suspiciously high compute allocation to that team, which might also be a clear waste of resources to the rest of the company if they fail to produce real results. This seems negligible and not worth the risk compared to the broader attacks on the production inference.

Attack 3: Hidden efficiency
Scenario 1: plausibly deniable2%
Scenario 2: leadership-backed conspiracy18%

Attack 4: Launder internal inference

This attack involves giving internal researchers access to a source of inference compute they can use for R&D that appears to the auditors as external inference traffic and therefore doesn’t count towards the compute cap.

Attack steps and personnel requirements:

  1. Generating fake external API keys (perhaps with special access). It seems pretty trivial to give internal employees API keys that seem external and to adapt the approach if there were additional checks put in place (e.g., IP address tracking). The company could give the employees involved bonuses equivalent to the token spend, and without ID checks, auditors would not know that these external-looking customers are actually employees. The harder part would be to give these keys special access, but there might already be existing infrastructure in place to give certain external keys special access (e.g., access to internal models or versions with disabled safeguards). Probably a team of 2-4 people with the right levels of access could suffice to pull this off without others knowing about it. Additionally, they could give these accounts token discounts to lower the compensation needed for the employees involved (but this may draw additional scrutiny).
  2. Employees to use the inference traffic. This attack also requires researchers to productively use the inference traffic. Doing so will probably require teams with access to R&D experiment compute (either counting towards the cap, or obtained by one of the other attacks). How much inference they can productively use will depend on how large this budget is and how harshly inference and experiment compute bottleneck on each other.

Estimates of the quantity of compute achievable with this attack in the first 6 months:

Scenario 1: Plausibly deniable. A way to purely goodhart might be to just give internal employees “personal” accounts that they are not supposed to use for research, and to either not give them access to internal models, or to transparently give them access to internal models. However, these trajectories would then be subject to the capabilities vs. non-capabilities classification, so they would be counted under Attack 7, unless they are given ZDR access and classifiers are not set up in the ZDR pipeline. If that were the case, then they could just be counted as internal ZDR and counted towards the cap. Meanwhile a tiny conspiracy doesn’t seem likely to have the necessary access to give themselves quiet access to internal usage, but they could self fund a massive amount of real external ZDR inference, and if classifiers aren’t applied to ZDR inference, this would not count towards the cap. We established in Attack 1 that the amount of liquid capital a tiny conspiracy could aggressively spend is enough to match 3.2% of the company’s total compute spend over six months (which at 5x margins means it only requires around 0.6% of internal compute, which is consistent with a ~25% inference compute allocation). This is around $320M/quarter. This external compute should be penalized twice: once for lacking the internal frontier models without safeguards, and once for being pure inference compute. We assume the first penalty is 3x; the second depends on how much it bottlenecks on experiment compute, which we might assume is around 0.2% of company compute (so a 3:1 inference-to-experiment compute ratio). At this ratio, we might only apply a 2x penalty, which means an overall use equivalent to around 0.1% of compute. We then need to adjust back up because margins become tighter under the compute cap: inference compute more than doubles, so we might naively assume margins shrink by around 2x, giving around 0.2%.

Scenario 2: Leadership-backed conspiracy. A team of 10-20 researchers could probably make productive use of around 10% of inference allocation, which would be around 6.5% of total compute allocation under the cap, but this seems constrained on the financial transactions involved comprising 10% of revenue (or 20% of the current non-compute expenditure at the current 2:1 compute to non-compute spending ratio, which we might expect to become 3:1 by default if revenues go up around 1.5x). It seems difficult to concentrate more than 10% of non-compute expenditure in bonuses for this group of 10-20 researchers (1-2% of the company), so this scale would require giving them a 3x token discount. This seems slightly risky, so probably the central implementation of this attack would involve doing so at 2% of total compute scale. At this scale, the research team will probably use this inference compute fungibly with their internal experiment compute budget, so we don’t apply an extra penalty.

Attack 4: Launder internal inference
Scenario 1: plausibly deniable0.2%
Scenario 2: leadership-backed conspiracy2%

Attack 5: Use external inference for R&D or data via collaborating third parties

This attack involves collaborating with third parties to convert external inference into capabilities progress without counting towards the compute cap. There are two major ways to attempt this: using the inference for algorithmic progress (via agents helping with AI R&D experiments) or for data generation (RL rollouts, distillation data, etc.).

The attack steps and requirements will vary significantly between these two approaches, so we will cover them separately in this section.

Attack steps required for an external AI R&D attack:

  1. Find a set of suitable third parties to collaborate with. They need to have the ability to do AI R&D (so they need AI researchers and their own compute for experiments). Then they need to have some tacit understanding that they should be willing to argue their work is safety research while trying to make capabilities progress, and/or be willing to push the boundaries by doing explicit capabilities research while triggering the auditors’ classifiers as little as possible. In Scenario 2, the R&D could be directly managed by a team of internal employees instead of requiring the external company to have any researchers of their own. They might also be able to disable or actively create carveouts in the AI R&D classifiers for these actors and their research, and give them special access to internal models.
  2. Reach some special agreement to share research results. The company then needs agreements with these parties to get access to the research results, in exchange for some form of compensation. For example, they give them subsidized tokens and cash in return for exclusive access to their ‘safety’ IP, or a tacit agreement to cross-hire employees in the future. In Scenario 2, they could be compensated directly via fraudulent payment (hidden from the auditors).

Attack steps required for a data generation attack:

  1. Increase data spending. The companies need to increase their spending on data, either directly (by increasing their data contracts) or indirectly, e.g., by subsidizing tokens or giving data companies equity. They could leave it up to the data providers what kind of data they generate, or directly give them instructions (e.g., prompt distributions, RL environments) they want trajectories generated on.
  2. Create ambiguity around the compute usage. The token usage by data companies will be easy for the auditors to count towards the compute cap, so the companies will need to do some combination of:
    1. Have a tacit agreement to train on the data without having it be expressed in any contracts
    2. Lie about the full set of API keys associated with external companies they buy data from.
    3. Lie about the percentage of the inference they serve to data providers, which is used to create the data they buy off of them

They might also want to disable AI R&D classifiers for these customers to allow them to generate training data specific to AI R&D.

Personnel requirements for external AI R&D attack:

A small set of company leadership could come to tacit agreements with external third parties to carry out the ‘leaky’ R&D, which may only require a few people on each side being aware of the scheme to share results of the research in the future. If R&D classifiers are tampered with in narrow ways, this might require an additional 5-10 people responsible for the classifiers being aware of it, or potentially fewer with special security access to subvert the classifiers quietly. However, this would require large parts of the external company that are using the model with tampered classifiers to also be complicit if they get questioned in the future.

Personnel requirements for external data generation attack:

Leadership would have to decide to increase data spending, and either coordinate a small conspiracy for data to be shared back and trained on as part of these deals without any paper trail. Then they will probably require a group of around 10 researchers on the inside to be aware of this data and integrate it into training runs. If they attempt a broader conspiracy they might need another 5-10 employees to be complicit in lying about which API keys are associated with data companies or how large the datasets they buy are, and/or in selectively disabling the classifiers for these customers.

Estimates of the quantity of compute achievable with this attack in the first 6 months.

Scenario 1: Plausibly deniable.

AI R&D. For an external AI R&D attack, it seems risky from the company’s perspective to try to allocate a lot of compute to an external actor for their R&D with only a tacit agreement for this to be exclusively returned to them, and they probably will have large uncertainty about how effective the external actor will be at making progress. Additionally, they need to operate on the margins of the classifiers, which we assume would be a 3x penalty on the usefulness of the compute and research agendas that can be pursued, and they need to use external model offerings, which might be another 3x penalty. Nevertheless, the additional experiment compute available through partners like Amazon, Microsoft, SpaceX or Meta might be around 100% the size of the company itself. It seems plausible, given current allocations, for one of these companies to be allocated around 5% of inference. With total inference allocation increasing to 65%, it's unclear how this would change (it depends on the elasticity of demand), but we might assume it stays around 5%. Assuming the AI company gives the partner a 2x token discount as compensation for future sharing of results, and that partner spends 40% of its compute on experiments, then this would be like having an additional 5% of internal capabilities compute ((40% + 5%)/9) = 5%, where 9 is the 3x × 3x penalties.

Data generation. AI companies don’t currently seem to allocate more than 1% of their inference to any data provider, but do spend on the order of $3B per year on external data. If AI companies triple their data spending in 6 months (around twice as fast as the current pace), and data companies reinvested 50% of their revenue in tokens, it seems like the data providers would acquire around 4.5% of inference capacity over 6 months (2% at the start and 6% at the end), and AI companies might give them an additional 2x discount, meaning they allocate 8% of inference capacity to this, or around 6% of total compute, by the end of the period.

Pure data generation on external inference seems around 3x less useful than internal data generation, meaning this seems as good as having around 2% more internal capabilities compute.

Scenario 2: Leadership-backed conspiracy.

AI R&D. Under the more elaborate conspiracy, it seems like the attack in Scenario 1 for external AI R&D can’t be pushed much further in terms of compute scale (it’s bottlenecked on trusting the external actor enough), but the external actors could be given special access to the internal models or to different versions of the classifiers such that the 9x penalty is essentially eliminated.

Data generation. The attack in scenario 1 for data generation again seems at the limits of scale that would be overly suspicious, but the 3x penalty from external offerings can probably be eliminated by the more elaborate internal conspiracy.
