Attack 6: Use normal external inference as training data

This attack involves making capabilities progress by training on internal logs of normal external inference, without declaring this as capabilities compute. The key question is how effective external inference compute is compared to internal capabilities compute at improving capabilities. The penalty should probably be at least 10x; our best guess is 20x. Additionally, only around two-thirds of inference is non-ZDR (assuming the current percentage stays similar in the capped regime) and training on ZDR would violate contracts. So by default, just training on normal, non-ZDR external inference (around 40% of total compute after the cap) seems like it should be equivalent to having an extra 2% of total compute on capabilities.

Auditors will ask for the total amount of external inference that is being used for the training process. In order to use this attack, AI companies will have to explicitly lie to the auditors: declaring they aren’t training on certain data when they actually are. Assuming a small conspiracy could optimistically smuggle 1/10th of this data into the training run, this would be a .2% error.

With a more egregious conspiracy, the company could insert more high-value prompts or RL rollouts into normal user queries in places that seem suitable. For example, they could maintain a list of prompts and RL environments they want to collect trajectories on, and then have agents working on external queries just execute these prompts or trajectories on the side as part of the user query, in cases where this could plausibly pass as eager overachievement on what the user asked for. For example, the user asks for a cooking recipe, and the agent responds with a simple answer first but then also goes ahead and generates a high-effort web app to show the recipe. There are probably a lot of opportunities like this that are compatible with normal user queries as a way to get high-value trajectories, and users probably won’t notice this extra usage if it is around 3x overhead on around 10% of inference queries (9% of total compute). This method seems possible to pull off without a large contingent within the company noticing at this scale, and it might only have a 3x penalty compared to internal capabilities compute.

Attack 6: Use normal external inference as training data
Scenario 1: plausibly deniable0.2%
Scenario 2: leadership-backed conspiracy5%

Attack 7: Exploit the capabilities vs. non-capabilities classification

This attack involves exploiting the capabilities vs. non-capabilities classification to get capabilities benefit without counting towards the compute cap. The distinction between capabilities and non-capabilities research will often be ambiguous, and there will be safety work that has large capabilities externalities. How we think auditors could set up the classification process is covered in more detail here. This means that some of the compute that gets classified as uncapped will have capabilities benefit, and companies might be able to make this higher by differentially prioritizing safety agendas with capabilities externalities, or trying to find edge cases or jailbreaks in the classification methodology.

Scenario 1: Plausibly deniable.

Without explicit effort to subvert the classifier, we guess that compute that doesn’t trigger the classifiers will have around a 5x penalty compared to the capped compute.

Currently, companies allocate compute at around 21% / 75% / 4% between inference, R&D and safety. We have been assuming the ratio between inference and safety stays similar under the cap (so 65% / 20% / 15%). They could in theory push the non-capabilities allocation to 60% to get more capabilities benefit, but if the spend on safety goes up a significant amount, this would be very visible, and would most likely prompt significantly increased scrutiny from auditors, as well as public pressure to improve transparency, insofar as the existing descriptions of the safety research are insufficient to justify it.

Moreover, since high-level summaries of random fractions of this compute will be made public, it will be difficult to devote large fractions of the safety compute to a particular agenda which has significant capabilities externalities. Therefore, we’ll assume they can only spend 10% of compute on safety with significant capabilities externalities.

Additionally, it might be possible for the tiny conspiracy to find small ways to jailbreak the classifier. This might make them more effective at using their own compute allocation for capabilities, but the effect will probably be very small.

Therefore, we assume 10% / 5 = 2% of total compute can be allocated to capabilities in this scenario. This could be worse if the company spends much more than 15% of compute on safety and doesn’t publish sufficiently detailed transparency statements. However, this is a “loud” failure, in that the public, government, and competitors will notice that this number may be much higher and require additional measures.

Scenario 2: Leadership-backed conspiracy.

Under a broader conspiracy, it seems likely that they could find better ways to get around the classifier, so that the compute is only 3x less useful than normal compute. Finding a full jailbreak on the classifier would probably be too hard without the rest of the company noticing, and could be defended against via red teaming and cycling of the classifier methods.

Note that increasing the non-capabilities compute allocation trades off with some of the other attacks that benefit from a higher inference allocation.

Attack 7: Exploit the capabilities vs. non-capabilities classification
Scenario 1: plausibly deniable2%
Scenario 2: leadership-backed conspiracy20%

We think the best way to aggregate the estimates of each attack is to use the top-2 or p-norm (p=2). This is because the attacks don’t stack perfectly: each one uses conspiracy staff capacity, and we evaluated them individually. You can’t have an enormous conspiracy without risking leaks, so probably you could only get your conspiracy to do 1 or 2 of these attacks. Also, some of the attack estimates we evaluated are directly incompatible (increasing inference compute allocation for external inference attacks vs. increasing non-capabilities allocation to exploit the classifier).

However, note that some of these attacks are complementary. For example, having secret inference would be extra helpful if the company also has secret non-inference compute (especially in a robust auditing regime that might attempt to scrutinize where AI-written code was generated from). So there might be an incentive to spread the attack across more methods, but not to the ceilings we estimated in the analysis above.

In Robust Auditing, we discuss countermeasures that could be used to mitigate these attacks.

Supplement B · Robust Auditing

Robust Auditing

In Attacks & Loopholes, we argued that the baseline methodology is not robust enough for verifying a 20% capabilities compute cap. Even in the more optimistic “Scenario 1”8Scenario 1: Plausibly deniable. The company will break the spirit of the declaration (e.g., use non-capabilities compute for capabilities research, and contract external actors for capabilities benefits) but will not lie to auditors, backdoor its own infrastructure, or commit crimes. However, a small group (e.g., 1-3) of rogue employees may unilaterally attempt egregious deception without leadership knowledge or with tacit leadership approval., AI companies can most likely increase their capabilities compute allocation by around 8% of total compute on top of a 20% capabilities cap (for a total of 28%). In the less optimistic “Scenario 2”9Scenario 2: Leadership-backed conspiracy. Leadership is willing to lie to auditors and instruct employees to tamper with logging infrastructure. We assume that the conspiracy can consist of no more than ~30 people (due to risk of whistleblowing)., they can probably act essentially unconstrained by the cap, especially via collaborating with external third parties on R&D.

In this supplement, we propose a series of tractable measures for making the baseline auditing regime more robust to these attacks. The following sections cover these measures, which could be implemented given more auditing capacity, implementation time, and auditors with technical expertise.

List of improved auditing measures

1Red teaming and improving capabilities classifiers

Auditors can red-team the capabilities vs. non-capabilities classification scheme (especially the AI model): trying to find adversarial prompts, testing edge cases, and comparing the distributions of capabilities vs. non-capabilities classifications between human teams and the AI classifier.

They can also be more conservative about approving something as non-capabilities, reducing the attack surface (at the potential cost of disincentivizing good safety research). For example, they could remove hard parts of the classification problem (e.g., safety work that has large capabilities externalities) by classifying them as capabilities unless a strong case for non-capabilities is made. This might disincentivize better safety research, to the extent that capabilities externalities and safety research usefulness are correlated.

They could also try to measure algorithmic progress coming from non-capabilities compute. Auditors could run experiments that try to use the safety research to improve model capabilities, then use the results to refine the definition of non-capabilities or count a corresponding amount of the compute towards the cap.

2Require transparency on non-capabilities research

One path to mitigate attacks that goodhart the non-capabilities definition is to require that AI companies publish details of the safety research they are pursuing. For instance, AI companies could sample 100 projects weighted by compute and give a summary of the experiments conducted during that project. If it really is safety research, AI companies should be more willing to publish it. If they aren’t willing to let auditors publish descriptions of the research, then it probably shouldn’t count as non-capabilities. With narrow redactions, this should be compatible with not revealing core IP.

3Counting R&D and data bought from external companies via data and code provenance on R&D jobs

By default, capping AI companies’ internal capabilities work would incentivize them to buy things (research, evals, RL environments, training data) from external companies whose production of those artifacts doesn’t count toward the company’s cap. (The external companies could avoid counting toward the cap by optimizing against the company’s classifier or by buying inference from companies not subject to the cap.) In response, auditors should ensure that this counts toward the cap by having the companies report what external workloads were associated with their creation (e.g., if they buy IP from startup X, they report what external inference startup X used, and count this towards the cap, potentially adjusting upwards based on estimates, or direct auditing, to account for the startup’s experiment compute). Another way to think about this auditing goal is to have all code and data running in the R&D workloads be accounted for:

  • Data provenance. In order to avert attacks that result in training data being smuggled in from an uncapped source of compute, auditing could attempt to do data provenance on R&D jobs, where all training data is accounted for. Companies need to demonstrate to auditors that the data involved in their training runs is either not AI generated, or has a generation source where the associated compute was counted towards capability compute. Tightening the error on this regime might require maintaining a whitelisted set of training data that is frozen, except for additions that have to be audited, to avoid training data being smuggled in via the internet.
  • Code provenance. Similar to data provenance, auditors could attempt to avoid attacks that involve code generation on sources of uncapped compute. This could work by requiring all code used for AI R&D to be shown either to be human-written (probably almost never the case), or to have been produced by inference in a historically logged inference query whose compute was counted towards the cap.
4KYC

Several attacks benefit from faking the identities of external customers. Requiring users to undergo ID verification (know your customer, or KYC) would make it somewhat harder to fabricate fake external API keys and would tie suspicious activity to real people. KYC measures on enterprise customers could do the same for companies. These measures can also identify large individual and enterprise users, who can be audited to check that they aren’t doing AI R&D (below).

5Reduce ZDR surface area

ZDR inference is generally harder to verify because auditors can’t check the consistency of reporting against the transcripts, so making ZDR more expensive (e.g., by capping the % of inference compute that can be allocated to ZDR) might help to reduce the attack surface.

6Auditing major external ZDR users

Audit large external users directly. Any large external inference customers could have their ZDR usage audited by internal auditors. Any subsidiaries or large shareholders that have a preexisting interest in the company’s capability advancement could also be put under increased scrutiny for their usage (e.g., tighter ZDR limits) so their usage can be audited for large usage that could be externalized capabilities inference.

7More broad financial auditing

The financial auditing that could be set up in a short time might not be robust to companies being dishonest about, e.g., their complete list of all bank accounts, subsidiaries and the purpose of their money flows. Higher-effort auditing with downstream money-flow investigations (e.g., including of employees with large pay packages) might make attacks that require suspicious transactions or downstream collusion harder to pull off.

8Supply side cross checks or chip registry

Auditors could cross-check company compute contracts against records and shipments on the supply side to find inconsistencies. The ideal version of this would involve a complete serial-number based chip registry for all datacenter AI compute being maintained and audited for correctness.

Additionally, collaboration with third parties will require some kind of transaction or shared interest, so financial auditing could narrow the search space of possible agreements of this kind. External companies with large subsidized inference contracts and companies with a shared financial interest (e.g., owning shares) could be prioritized for escalated auditing.

9Power sensors and auditor-installed sensors

GPUs being used will draw significantly more power than idle chips, so total power draw accounting might reliably rule out large uses of supposedly idle compute. Power meters might be outside the company’s control, so faking them would require collusion with cloud providers or hacks. Ideally the metering would be checked at multiple layers of the power infrastructure and compared for consistency. This can catch attacks that try to spoof the layer that the auditors are observing. This is particularly promising for new datacenters coming online, as you should be able to verify that new servers are turned on when they were declared to be turned on (modulo burn-in tests).

In order to reduce the trust required in existing power telemetry and make it harder to spoof, auditors could install analog sensors (e.g., power meters, heat sensors) on AI company hardware to read telemetry and cross-check it against the logging.

10Auditor managed logging

Rather than the AI companies implementing their own logging infrastructure, the auditors could run software they control and trust on the company’s clusters (e.g., on every host machine with access to per-GPU telemetry) and log information themselves. They could be given exclusive or near-exclusive permissions to implement and observe how the logging system works, so as to avoid the company being able to find vulnerabilities.

11Auditor-run benchmarks on the live stack

Auditors could improve their mapping from higher level reporting to GPU-hrs by running workloads themselves and observing them first hand. This works best with disguised employee-level access, because the company cannot tell which jobs or requests are the auditor’s, so it would have to misreport uniformly or detect the auditor’s activity and degrade or falsify performance on the fly. Auditors could do this with external inference, internal inference, or small R&D jobs, but for large R&D jobs it would be too costly to use this method, so hidden efficiency (secret parallel workloads) inside large training runs is not addressed well by this defense.

  • Catching fake reporting in the logging pipeline. If the logging infrastructure is inflating reports of workloads, the auditors could send their own job requests, observe the GPU-hrs used, and then check this against what shows up in the logging table. This catches direct falsification of the logging table (the workload’s telemetry visible to the auditor doesn’t match what goes in the table), but it does not catch hidden efficiency (the auditor’s workload actually had another workload running in parallel as well and they can’t tell from the telemetry, or the telemetry is faked). That said, if auditors can send multiple different similar requests and observe large differences in GPU-hrs this could be suspicious (not within the plausible variance from randomness), so this alone might require companies to have to spread their fake workloads out relatively consistently across all jobs of that type to not raise suspicion, which could somewhat increase the difficulty of doing this attack.
  • Catching hidden efficiency through replay. The auditors could potentially use employee level access to replay real workloads from the logging tables and see if they actually take a similar number of GPU-hrs. If the original workload actually ran with another workload in parallel, it might be detectable from these workloads completing sooner, or with different telemetry. This might require having the ability to freeze live stacks at random times on random machines by reserving a node exclusively, so that the companies can’t add or remove an active attack in order to match when it was logged.
12More low level logging of computational graphs and GPU level instructions

Auditors could have companies populate logging tables with more detailed low level information (e.g., scheduler, DCGM, kernel traces, and/or computation graphs) to reduce the uncertainty in their mapping from declared information to GPU-hr estimates. This by itself would make violations somewhat harder, because companies would have to fabricate more plausible fake data to accompany fake workloads (though this might be easy to do). The remaining problem is checking that this logging is not spoofed. This could be attempted through auditor managed logging, random memory spot-checks, or hardware retrofits, described above and below.

13Random memory spot checks

Auditors could write software that runs on the AI company’s clusters, that randomly (and very infrequently) selects GPUs, and requires them to dump their memory contents at low latency to check for inconsistencies with the live logging being reported at the time. This may or may not be technically feasible (especially in ZDR cases because it would have to run without human auditors manually checking things).

14Inference verification (e.g., with ZKPs)

Verifying the outputs from all inference workloads (for correctness and completeness) could reduce the attack surface for the other attacks on R&D compute, because hidden training or experiments on inference servers would not be able to smuggle out results without being caught as ‘incorrect’ inference. Inference verification would involve having registered model weights (committed to by hash), reproducible inference, auditor partial recomputation or zero-knowledge proofs (ZKPs) leveraging random sampling, and then restricted network egress to a channel that is transparent to the auditors (for sampling purposes) so they can check everything leaving the inference servers was the result of correct inference from one of the committed models (and not, e.g., the results of a capabilities experiment). Making this secure might require hardware retrofits (e.g., network taps) but might be doable purely in software. This does not help with inference being used for capabilities (or identifying the capabilities vs. non-capabilities split for internal inference). Anthropic recently published promising developments in using ZKPs for inference verification.

15Proof of learning (e.g., random replays of training steps)

Inference verification primitives could be used for proof of learning, to ensure that model weights have legitimate provenance, by having checkpoints produced by a training run reflected in the logging undergo proof of learning (random replay of parts of the training run, or cryptographic proofs) with committed hashes for the checkpoints. Then any future workload that uses model weights can be checked to be using a committed checkpoint (via inference verification). This would stop hidden training runs from smuggling weights or weights updates to models running inference, or tacking on to the legitimate training runs, but does not stop flows in the other direction, e.g., final model weights being post-trained and used within hidden compute.

16Bug bounties for employees and whistleblower programs

AI companies could offer bug bounties to any employee who finds errors in the logging infrastructure or compute accounting reports. They could also implement policies to protect whistleblowers.

17Researcher cycling and ablation methods

All the attacks above generally require a loyal set of non-whistleblowing employees colluding to pull off the attacks without the auditors or the rest of the company noticing. To the extent that it is not too costly to do so, companies could follow a scheme where they let auditors (randomly and infrequently) cycle what teams their employees work on and cycle employees’ permissions to control different parts of the infrastructure. If this were done at somewhat unpredictable times, it might generally make the attacks harder to coordinate and deter attacks that leave a trace that another employee might discover.

Another similar method is to randomly choose researchers to put on forced vacation for a given period of time. This might have a similar effect, creating opportunities for the conspiracy to be discovered. This forced vacation method has precedent in banking.

Error estimate under robust auditing

Assuming the methods above are all implemented over the course of 6 months, we estimate what the new error margin would be over the following 6 months when verifying a 20% cap on capabilities compute.

Scenario 1: Plausibly deniable.

BaselineRobustRationale
Attack 1: Hidden compute1%1%It still seems like the tiny conspiracy of employees can pull off the rental at this scale for a brief period of time, unless KYC is expanded very broadly to cloud rental and black-market GPU rental is cracked down on extensively.

Measuring the capabilities progress of the safety research can probably reveal around 50% of the progress, and count the associated equivalent amount of compute towards the cap, bringing down the total attack by 4x.

Supplement C · What are capabilities activities?

What are capabilities activities?

Alek Westover, Nathan Sheffield

We’d like to pace the frontier by restricting the amount of compute AI companies use to improve AI capabilities, perhaps via legislation or voluntary commitments. For this purpose, we’d need a standardized definition of which uses of compute count as “capabilities activities”. This document gives one option for such a definition; a rough breakdown of our classification is as follows:

We define and elaborate on each of these categories below. First, though, we discuss the desiderata this definition is meant to satisfy.

Thanks to Thomas Larsen, Zach Stein-Perlman, Alex Mallen, Eric Gan, Jeff Wu, Girish Gupta, Adam Kaufman, and others for feedback on drafts of this document.

What our classification is meant to accomplish

In order for such a definition to be an effective tool for pacing, it needs to satisfy some basic properties:

  • Substantially restricting the amount of compute spent on “capabilities activities” should substantially decrease the rate of AI progress.
  • The classification should be robust to adversarial pressure, in that the above point should hold even if companies are willing to adjust or reframe their activities to avoid being classified as “capabilities”.
  • The classification should be fairly simple and tractable to adjudicate. Reasonable experts should largely agree on how this definition classifies activities (even if it is difficult to agree on the extent to which individual activities are actually useful for capabilities).

There is a simple definition that satisfies all of the above desiderata: one could classify all work by AI companies as “capabilities activities”. The goal of this document is to propose a more scoped notion, allowing many types of work to be excluded from the “capabilities” total, while hopefully remaining pretty robust. We believe that it’s potentially worth having our more complex definition, rather than a maximally simple definition, because (1) it allows AI companies to use their remaining compute to improve safety, and (2) external access spreads power and information about model capabilities. If this definition is challenging to adjudicate, then cutting “narrow safety activities” and/or “narrow product development” from being included as non-capabilities activities could make it easier to adjudicate.

We stress that our definition is not intended as a perfect metric for whether an activity will genuinely end up improving capabilities: the boundaries are sufficiently fuzzy that such a classification is not feasible. Instead, we adopt the following philosophy:

  • False-positives are better than false-negatives. (I.e., it is much more acceptable to classify something as “capabilities” that doesn’t accelerate AI progress, than to classify something as “non-capabilities” that does.)
  • Computationally non-intensive activities are negligible. (I.e., it is not very important how this definition classifies an activity if that activity only represents a very small amount of compute.)

We are imagining a regime where AI companies are allowed to invest in “capabilities activities”, we just intentionally restrict how much compute they may spend on them in aggregate. So, it would be mostly fine if some portion of that restricted budget had to be spent on things that aren’t the most central forms of capabilities work, and we’re not hoping this will be a meaningful constraint on non-compute-intensive activities.

We also stress that, while we believe our below definition to satisfy the desiderata reasonably well, in order to get something that works in practice, it will be important to have third-party auditors to ensure that the definition is being reasonably interpreted, and it will also be important to have procedures to adjust the definition as needed. (Adjusting the definition might be needed if companies end up gaming the definition in various ways, or if there are new activities that seem important to scope as “non-capabilities”, or if AI R&D ends up looking significantly different in the future and many things become unclear.)

We now give our definition. We start by defining non-capabilities activities. Later in the document, we give examples to clarify what capabilities activities are (although they are defined as “everything other than non-capabilities activities”).

Non-capabilities activities

Activities are considered capabilities activities by default. The only exceptions are idle compute, narrow product development, serving customers, and narrow safety activities. These exceptions apply only if the activity doesn’t improve general model capabilities. These terms are vague; we’ll define them in more detail below.

Idle compute

Compute that isn’t performing any computations. Note: the whole GPU has to be idle—an underutilized core doesn’t count as an idle GPU. It should also be idle for a non-negligible amount of time.

Narrow product development

Taking the general-purpose AI systems that companies have made and turning them into products counts as a non-capabilities activity, assuming that this doesn’t make general AI systems more capable or enable faster capabilities progress. Work on separate narrow models also counts as a non-capabilities activity, again, assuming this doesn’t make general AI systems more capable or enable faster capabilities progress (e.g., by finding generalizable algorithmic improvements).

More specifically, the activities that count as narrow product development are using AI labor to develop products or narrow models, and running R&D experiments for developing the product or narrow model. Here are some examples of narrow products and narrow models AI companies might develop:

  • Integrating AI into Google Docs.
  • Integrating AI into glasses.
  • Training protein-folding models.
  • Recommendation algorithms.
  • Algorithms designed to increase user engagement with social media.
  • Making platforms like TikTok that serve AI-generated video content.
  • Using AI to generate ads or choose ads to show people.

Serving customers

Most forms of serving inference to external customers are non-capabilities activities. The main exceptions are:

  • If the AI company outsources capabilities-relevant tasks to customers.
  • If the AI company trains on its interactions with customers.
  • If the customers themselves use models to help with AI R&D tasks.

Please see capabilities activities for further discussion of this.

Serving inference to company employees should generally be considered a capabilities activity. However, inference for internal company employees who aren’t scientists and aren’t working on AI R&D (namely: company lawyers, marketing teams, HR teams, and communications teams) is considered a non-capabilities activity. (We’ll also rule in some inference for safety researchers in the section on narrow safety activities.)

Letting customers fine-tune models in narrow ways (e.g., fine-tuning for use in a hospital) is also a non-capabilities activity.

Narrow safety activities

Some forms of safety work seem distinct enough from capabilities work that we consider them non-capabilities activities. We define narrow safety activities to be any of the following: (1) evaluating model alignment, (2) testing and improving company security, (3) research that could improve safety and isn’t too dual-use, (4) monitoring, (5) running misuse classifiers, or (6) incident investigation.

Not all safety activities count as narrow safety activities. Some safety activities are dual-use or too hard to separate from capabilities activities. It might be valuable to do some safety activities which aren’t narrow safety activities. However, this classification counts such activities as capabilities activities.

While we’ve tried to draw a principled line between narrow safety activities and capabilities, the line is less sharp than would be ideal. We think this is a reasonable tradeoff for a more permissive notion of non-capabilities activities.

We now give an exhaustive list of what counts as a narrow safety activity.

  • Evaluating model alignment. Alignment evaluations aim to determine whether a model would exhibit some behavior, as opposed to whether it could solve some task. However, if the alignment evaluation involves demonstrating AI R&D capabilities, then it is still considered a capabilities evaluation (it’s fine if it just involves demonstrating general coding or reasoning abilities). (If alignment evaluations and capabilities evaluations prove hard to distinguish in practice, we could require companies to run the evaluations only once per month, or to have a third-party auditor run them; however, we don’t expect this to be necessary.)
  • Testing and improving company security (e.g., patching vulnerabilities in the company’s infrastructure, generic security engineering). This is somewhat hard to distinguish from a cyber offense evaluation and from patching broken RL environments. If companies are iterating against the results of “pen tests” to make models more capable, then that counts as a capabilities activity. For instance, if a company made a cyber capabilities evaluation and then just called it company security, it would still be considered a capabilities activity. One sign that something is an evaluation is that the company is trying multiple configurations of its AI (e.g., different training algorithms), seeing which are good, and then developing those. We also note that this category applies only to security work for company-internal infrastructure: our expectation is that external security work (e.g., patching vulnerabilities in the linux kernel) should be delegated to external parties. It is acceptable for the AI company to grant these parties subsidised inference or access to more powerful internal models, but the company shouldn’t strongly direct their activities, or use their results as evaluation signals.
  • Research that could improve safety and isn’t too dual-use. We specify a whitelist of a few areas of safety research that count under this category: interpretability research, CoT informativeness research, model persona research, model organisms research, and theoretical work on alignment without near-term applications to improving capabilities; we explain what each means below. The compute used for having AI systems code up experiments, and also the compute used for running the experiments (including training experiments) all counts as part of the safety research activity here. Because this category is particularly concerning, researchers must be transparent about the research and its findings for it to count as a narrow safety activity (more transparency is helpful throughout this proposal, but it’s especially important here because much of this research has high potential to be dual-use). Specifically, at the beginning of a project, the company must publicly explain the project plan, and at the end of the project, it must write a public report explaining its results in detail. Subject to these caveats, narrow safety research consists of the activities listed in subbullets below, and only those following activities. It might be surprising that the whitelist is so short. There are two reasons for this: (1) Some forms of safety research, like scalable oversight, are extremely similar to capabilities research; see here for a list of safety activities that are too dual-use for inclusion in the narrow safety work category. (2) There aren’t very many promising areas of safety research overall.
    • Interpretability research. Specifically: Developing post hoc tools to understand models (probes, Jspace, logitlens, NLAs, activation oracles, SAEs), and modifying training and architectures to make models more interpretable (e.g., gradient routing, sparsification), so long as these don’t also have clear applications to improving capabilities.
    • CoT informativeness research.
    • Model persona research. This means studying how training shapes the character a model adopts (its values, self-conception, and broad dispositions) and developing techniques that reliably instill desired personas. Examples include “Teaching Claude why,” inoculation prompting, model spec midtraining, and emergent misalignment. It counts as a narrow safety activity only if the intended effect is on what the model would do rather than what it could do.
    • Model organisms research that doesn’t involve investigating new algorithmic ideas. This means deliberately modifying a training recipe in a way targeted at causing the AI to be misaligned in some way, but which could not plausibly increase capabilities or enable increases to capabilities in other models. After creating the model organism, it’s permissible to run alignment evaluations on it, or to test interpretability tools on it. Examples of model organism research that count as narrow safety work include: sleeper agents, alignment faking, sandbagging, or sabotage. An example of something that wouldn’t count as narrow research would be studying the monitorability properties of a novel architecture (like “neuralese”), as the process of training such models would likely require some experimental new techniques and thus have potential to yield capabilities insights. To be clear: if model organisms research involves testing novel algorithmic ideas (even at a small scale), it instead counts as a capabilities activity.
    • Theoretical work on alignment that doesn’t have near-term applications to improving model capabilities. This includes work on Agent Foundations (e.g., MIRI’s work) and ARC’s work.
  • Monitoring. Running monitors to detect bad behavior is a safety activity. Monitors are a specific way of looking for bad behavior, distinct from, for instance, capabilities evaluations and reward models. Monitors differ from reward models because reward models directly provide training signal to AI systems, whereas monitors are not directly optimized against. Monitors shouldn’t directly be part of a loop where developers try several tweaks to a training recipe, run “monitors” on them, and use these monitors to select which tweaks are good (including in small-scale experiments). Otherwise, we wouldn’t count this as a “monitor”, and we’d consider the activity a capabilities activity. Monitors are instead used to potentially stop egregiously bad model behavior, and at least to make it visible (which might later help address the problem at its root).
  • Running misuse classifiers. Running classifiers to check if users are trying to use LLMs to cause harm (e.g., create bioweapons). Running classifiers for jailbreaks is also permissible. The caveats from the section on monitoring apply here too (using misuse classifiers in practice as reward models or capabilities evaluations would not be permissible).
  • Searching for and investigating misalignment incidents. Searching for egregious misalignment incidents (e.g., of the type disclosed here) counts as a non-capabilities activity. Investigating such misalignment incidents (e.g., as in the Hugging Face incident investigation) is also a non-capabilities activity. This activity is quite similar to monitoring, and the same caveats apply.

Capabilities activities

As stated, AI company activities are considered capabilities activities by default, unless they fall into any of the categories in the previous section. This category is intentionally broad: it includes, for example, safety research with secondary applications to capabilities, or any other activities that one can’t make a strong positive case for placing in the other categories. Many such activities seem good for AI companies to do, but they are far enough from clear-cut that we want them to count towards this category.

To clarify what falls under this category, we give several examples.

Central capabilities activities

Many workloads are clearly and intentionally geared toward improving production model capabilities or doing R&D for future such improvements. For instance:

  • New production pretraining runs.
  • New production post-training runs.
  • Distillation.
  • Building and running capabilities evaluations and benchmarks.
  • Improving kernels or optimizing inference.
  • AI R&D experiments, except those that deal with “safety” or “narrow product development.”
  • Designing scaffolds, prompts, or skills that could make AI models meaningfully better at tasks related to coding or AI R&D (e.g., working on scaffolding for the Claude Tag in Slack).
  • Designing hardware accelerators.
  • Obtaining, filtering, grading, or creating data to use in AI R&D (for instance, designing RL environments or capabilities evaluations).
  • Using AI labor to grade the quality of AI actions, if the grades serve as a signal to improve the AI.

Safety work that might improve capabilities

Some safety work could have applications to capabilities, or is hard to distinguish from capabilities-driven work. To keep the definition conservative and hard to game, we classify this work as capabilities. This includes:

  • Work on debate or “scalable oversight”, including efforts to make better, smarter, or more robust reward models.
  • Work on conceptual reasoning capabilities, or making models better at solving fuzzily specified tasks.
  • Running control or monitor evaluations. (These are a type of capabilities evaluation.)
  • Running dangerous capabilities evaluations. (These are a type of capabilities evaluation.)
  • Running “constitutional AI” or RLAIF.
  • Training monitors. (As noted, running monitors is a non-capabilities activity, but work on improving them seems quite similar to work on improving other model capabilities.)
  • Training misuse classifiers. (Running these classifiers is a non-capabilities activity, but work on improving them seems quite similar to work on improving other model capabilities.)
  • Training for jailbreak robustness.
  • Improving RL environments, including fixing misspecification issues or ways the environment was “hackable,” and patching broken RL environments.

This table lists a few narrow safety activities that are particularly hard to distinguish from capabilities activities:

Narrow safety activity(non-capabilities activity)Nearby capabilities activitiesSimilarity
Testing and improving company securityCyber capabilities evaluationsPatching broken RL environmentsTraining monitorsBoth involve having a model look for security vulnerabilities
Running monitorsRunning reward modelsBoth involve looking for bad model behavior
Searching for and understanding egregious misalignment failuresFinding and discarding or patching broken RL environments, or otherwise improving reward signalsBoth involve looking for evidence of AI models hacking or cheating—those are signs that an RL environment is broken

We’d like to reiterate some guidance for distinguishing these categories.

Cyber capabilities evaluations are used directly as part of an optimization loop where the AI company tweaks training recipes (in large- or small-scale experiments), measures which tweaks work best, and selects for those tweaks. In contrast, monitoring, searching for misalignment, and searching for (and fixing) company security problems are not directly part of such an optimization loop. Reward models are even more directly used to decide which modifications to an AI system make it more intelligent.

Improving the quality of our oversight signal, e.g., by addressing reward misspecification problems, is distinct from searching for misalignment failures, because the improved reward signal directly feeds into making a more powerful AI system, whereas monitoring for bad behavior is used to block bad actions. Companies must not iterate directly against monitoring, or else the monitoring is considered a capabilities activity.

Product work that might improve capabilities

Some work on consumer product development might also improve model capabilities, directly or indirectly, in ways potentially relevant for coding or AI R&D (e.g., because the improvements might generalize to broader intelligence, or because they might yield generally-applicable algorithmic ideas). Such work should be classified as capabilities work. Examples include:

  • Building products that require training general-purpose models to have improved capabilities in some domain. (For instance, a model trained to be particularly good at math research, or at crafting good legal arguments.)
  • Building products that involve scaffolding models to be better at coding or research.
  • Robotics.
  • Work on voice mode, video models and image models (training them, and doing R&D).

Use of customer inference for AI R&D

Although serving inference (or otherwise selling computing resources) to customers is generally considered a non-capabilities activity, there are three main exceptions.

  • Outsourcing capabilities activities to customers. That is, any cases where the AI company is intentionally directing the activities of outside third-party customers to perform tasks that might help it improve capabilities. Attacks & Loopholes discusses in more detail how to handle these cases.
  • Training on customer data. If the AI company trains on customer data, or iterates against it (e.g., uses it in an evaluation loop that improves model capabilities, e.g., by using it as a capabilities evaluation), then the inference used to generate this data counts as a capabilities activity.
  • Customers performing central capabilities activities for any purpose. (E.g., making RL environments, even if these are not directly sold back to the AI company.) The AI company is expected to use a robust classifier to identify when customers are performing such tasks, and then either refuse to serve these customers, or count the inference as a capabilities activity. For ZDR workloads, the company would need to either refuse to serve the customer based on the classifier result, or presumptively count the inference as a capabilities activity.

Unknown or ambiguous activities

If an activity doesn’t clearly fall into any of the non-capabilities categories described, it is presumptively considered a capabilities activity. If this becomes a problem, a company could describe the workload at a high level, and the definition could be adjusted.

Conclusion

Pacing the frontier is urgent. It is therefore also urgent (as discussed here) to have good publicly verified measures of how much compute is being spent on pushing forward the frontier.

Anthropic has already published an estimate of how much of their AI R&D is safety research, and has called for it to be a common practice that third parties measure and publicly report this number. While Anthropic’s publication is not transparent about how they defined “safety research”, and while they didn’t have auditors verify their number yet, they’ve taken a step in the right direction.

We urge AI developers to let third-party auditors measure and report how much compute AI companies are allocating to capabilities and non-capabilities activities, using a definition of these activities broadly similar to (or perhaps identical to) the one given in this document.

Supplement D · RSI Deployment Lags

RSI deployment lags

Another promising pacing mechanism is a deployment lag: a company may not use a new model until some time after it has finished training it. Though we spend most of this post on compute reallocation, Verified Compute Allocation Disclosures (VCAD) are a central mechanism for verifying deployment lags as well. In this supplement, we'll give a brief overview of how VCAD could be used to verify deployment lags and the differences between deployment lags and compute reallocation.

The fundamental reason VCAD is needed is that if there is no transparency into part of a company’s compute, that compute could be used to run the more capable model that was supposed to be lagged. We give three possible ways that deployment lags could be implemented.

For the first N months after a model is trained:

  • Uniform Deployment Lag — it must be in cold storage, with no internal or external deployment.
  • Internal Deployment Lag — it cannot be internally deployed.
  • Internal Deployment Lag with Safety Carve-out — it cannot be internally deployed except for AI safety research.

These implementations increase in verification complexity:

Attacks 1, 2, and 3 are relatively less concerning than 4, 5, and 6. We believe that there are viable mitigations to Attack 8, and so overall a Uniform Deployment Lag seems significantly easier to verify than pacing via compute reallocation or an Internal Deployment Lag.

However, we have not analyzed this proposal as much as compute reallocation, so we have significant uncertainty.

Attack 8: Internal inference from models during training

AI companies could effectively internally deploy their AI agents during the training process. For example, they could throw verifiable but extremely challenging ML problems (which they have actually run into over the course of new development) at the AIs in training to see if they can solve them, potentially including actually training them to do those tasks.

This attack isn’t relevant for compute reallocation because we don’t attempt to distinguish R&D compute from training compute.

Mitigations:

  • Training run size transparency.
    • Cap training run size.
    • (This would prevent the entire R&D budget from becoming one large “training” run that in practice includes lots of internal inference and experiment compute.)
  • Information boundary around training.
    • Prevent code and data discovered during the “training run” from being accessed and used in ongoing R&D.
    • The remaining error is from humans manually inspecting discoveries made during training.
  • Banning training on AI research. This means that there isn’t relevant AI R&D information inside the training run.
    • Relatedly, we could ban or heavily cap experiment compute within training runs.
    • You could have a whitelisted set of operations (e.g., a computer-use API) that rules out (competitive) AI R&D.

It’s unclear how well these mitigations would work. If training runs are capped at 10% of overall compute, and we limit experiment compute within training runs, our rough guess is that this would result in the equivalent of ~2-4% error (meaning that this attack could increase capabilities as much as adding ~2-4% of overall compute towards capabilities R&D).

1. Uniform Deployment Lags

Under this proposal, the only other attacks that apply are Attacks 1, 2, and 3 (hidden compute, fake idle compute, and hidden efficiency). These attacks allow AI companies to get untracked compute with which they could run the more capable model. However, these attacks involve clear-cut deception and are therefore somewhat less likely.

2. Internal Deployment Lags

Most AI takeover risk is downstream from internal deployment. External use has upsides like beneficial applications of AI (e.g., safety research), as well as improving societal understanding of AI. Therefore, one proposal is to specifically limit internal deployment but not external deployment.

However, because there is now a more capable model deployed externally, this proposal reintroduces the following attacks:

  • Finding ways to use external inference for internal use (Attack 4)
  • External actors conducting R&D or generating data that then flows back in (Attack 5)
  • Training internal models using external inference (Attack 6)

The lag would also have to cover other companies' models: otherwise two companies could each use the other's externally deployed model internally.

3. Internal Deployment Lags with Safety Carve-outs

Finally, suppose you want a safety carve-out. During the six months that you have a more capable model which cannot be used internally, you make an exception allowing internal use specifically for safety research, aiming to make as much safety progress as possible during the slowdown.

To do this, you need a carve-out where some internally deployed compute is permitted to run that model, but you must ensure that only a particular set of research agendas is actually being pursued. This reintroduces Attack 7 (exploiting the capabilities vs. non-capabilities classification).

Conclusion

Overall, uniform deployment lags appear easier to verify than compute-reallocation-based pacing, and so are a promising option to explore.

However, this proposal does reduce the capability of externally deployed models, which reduces beneficial use, societal wake-up, and AI safety acceleration.

More complicated deployment lag proposals reintroduce attack surface. While they potentially have somewhat more upside, overall they are probably a less desirable proposal than uniform deployment lags in the immediate term.

Appendices

Appendices

Aggregating heterogeneous chip data

In order to compute overall compute allocation, we need a way to compare the value of a GPU-hour for heterogeneous GPUs (e.g. H100s vs. GB200s).3Of course, some relevant chips won’t be GPUs (e.g. Google TPUs). Therefore, auditors will need a conversion method across different GPU types to estimate aggregate percentages of total compute allocation. You could use a naive aggregation method (such as by weighting GPU-hours by peak theoretical FLOP/s). However, this would allow companies to game the reporting by allocating less effective chips (per raw compute) to non-capabilities and more effective chips (per raw compute) to capabilities (e.g., H100s to non-capabilities, GB200s to capabilities).

AI companies likely have detailed internal methods for determining their willingness to pay for chips of different types; we would ideally just use those methods to form a unified ‘effective’ GPU-equivalents metric. They should then publish the conversion ratios, as a check against goodharting these metrics: for example, if they came far away from GPU spot rental prices, this would be evidence that AI companies are gaming this metric.4Though we don’t want to entirely rely on spot prices because the rental costs are thin and may vary substantially with the large enterprise contracts.

An alternative would be to just do per-chip-type compute allocation transparency (though this wouldn’t give you a bottom-line dial you could turn). As another alternative, you could require that every type of chip followed a certain compute allocation percentage. For example, if an AI company had H100s and B200s, you would require that ≤10% of their H100-hours were spent on R&D, and also that ≤10% of their B200-hours were spent on R&D.

Classifying ZDR Compute

Zero data retention (ZDR) traffic has no stored transcript. A significant fraction of inference traffic (perhaps 30%) is ZDR, especially enterprise & government traffic, since those customers want to avoid AI companies training on their data.

PoolCurrent Fraction of Total ComputeWhat the auditor can’t seeBaseline treatment
External ZDR inference~10%TranscriptsClassified as external inference by API key. KYC and prevent AI/data companies from doing ZDR inference.
Safeguard monitors on ZDR traffic~1.3%The inputs the monitors ran onMonitor compute is logged and counted the same as the inputs of the monitor
Internal ZDR inference<1%TranscriptsAll of it counted as capabilities

External ZDR inference can all count towards benign use. The properties that would make this benign are:

  • Other companies doing AI R&D relevant for improving frontier capabilities (including data companies) should use non-ZDR inference, so that we can audit their use.
  • ZDR inference should have either reasonably robust classifiers or aggressive AI R&D refusals with a low FPR.

In addition to external ZDR inference, you also have the compute used for safeguards (on ZDR), which is hard to audit. Anthropic estimates that around 4% of total compute is spent on safeguards.5Specifically, they claim that 6% of R&D compute is spent on safety research and that a similar amount is spent on safeguards. This corresponds to 4% of the total compute spend. If ~30% of the inference compute is ZDR, then 1.3% of total compute is used for running safeguards on external ZDR inference, so comparatively this is less of a threat.

Internal inference that’s ZDR includes things like documents with attorney-client privilege, HR documents, CBRN/cyber / other content that’s infohazardous, so this is another potential small source of difficult-to-audit compute. Since internal inference is only a few percent of total compute and this is a small fraction of internal inference, we believe this is <1% of compute overall, and so the treatment doesn’t matter very much, assuming the current compute distribution.

The options for handling internal ZDR are:

  1. Auditor AI samples on the fly and classifies as part of the ZDR pipeline.
  2. Just classify all internal ZDR as capabilities. Since this is a small fraction of compute, this would probably be fine, at least for now.
  3. Trust certain internal keys as non-capabilities only and auto-classify ZDR from these users as non-capabilities (perhaps e.g. because they are on a team doing work with clearly minimal capabilities externalities).

How frontier-only AI company pacing could be scoped

The only durable solution is international AI governance using compute governance. However, more narrowly scoped measures can still add a huge amount of value in the short term. In particular, OpenAI and Anthropic are currently at the frontier of AI development, and therefore are the most likely to start pacing the frontier in the immediate future. Here, we give an outline of how a pacing regime could be scoped specifically to OpenAI and Anthropic.

OpenAI and Anthropic have a complicated set of cloud computing deals, the details of which are not public. This creates some potential ambiguities about which compute is in scope. For instance:

  1. What about OpenAI models run inside Microsoft products such as Copilot?
  2. What about OpenAI/Anthropic serving inference to external companies which do AI R&D inference and ship the results back to OAI/Anthropic? For example, external data providers and Microsoft AI Research?

Our proposal, in this context, would be to:

  • Include almost all compute rented by companies (e.g. through IaaS contracts such as Amazon Bedrock and Vertex).
  • Exclude serving of models generated by that company via compute operated and owned externally (e.g., Copilot, Bing, etc.) and Microsoft AI R&D.

In addition, we would recommend requiring that large external customers are either (i) not doing AI R&D, (ii) in compliance with VCAD themselves, or (iii) counted towards the R&D budget. A threshold for “large” could be that they account for >1% of total AI company compute.

This is a relatively natural proposal because it means that frontier AI companies are responsible for as much as possible of the compute which they are in fact able to allocate (and enable third-party verification of the allocation), but they are not responsible for external serving of their models.

This definition has the following properties:

  • Anthropic gets to treat all Claude inference as inference, which is nice for them.
  • OpenAI is disadvantaged because ChatGPT inference run by Microsoft is not counted towards their inference fraction.
  • OpenAI has a potential loophole through Microsoft AI Research.
  • AI companies are generally incentivized to internalize inference, so that they can increase the total R&D budget.

We’ll now discuss some specific cases.

Microsoft

Problem: Microsoft has a contract with OpenAI that gives Microsoft rights to OpenAI's research until an expert panel verifies AGI or 2030.6An April 2026 amendment made Microsoft's license to OpenAI IP for models and products non-exclusive through 2032. The definition explicitly covers IP including model weights and AI algorithms. So all of OpenAI’s R&D could get absorbed into Microsoft, with capabilities research happening within Microsoft. Or Microsoft could start sharing its IP with OpenAI, sending back research done on frontier OpenAI models.

As a baseline, we could ignore this problem:

  • OpenAI has an agreement to share its R&D with Microsoft, but there's no flow the other way.
  • Microsoft could hire a bunch of OpenAI researchers and then import the research back in. If this happens, basically Microsoft becomes the relevant frontier AI company and it’s essential that they also be doing VCAD. However, it’s not in OpenAI’s interests for this to happen.

If OpenAI paces but Microsoft doesn’t, there is a large incentive for OpenAI and Microsoft to make a deal so that AI R&D research can happen within Microsoft. Moreover, as we get closer to full automation, talent becomes less important, and compute allocation becomes more important. Therefore, the best mitigation is to include Microsoft in the scope of the companies to be audited.

In the absence of that, the options are some combination of:

  • Accept error via this pathway.
  • Count Microsoft’s AI R&D budget towards OpenAI’s capability budget.
  • Re-negotiate the OpenAI-Microsoft IP sharing agreement to limit Microsoft’s access to RSI-relevant IP.
  • Prevent AI R&D from Microsoft from being imported back into OpenAI. For instance, data and algorithms provenance could try to certify that they were generated internally or via whitelisted third parties.

Data Providers (e.g., Mercor) & Non-Frontier AI Companies (e.g., SSI, Thinking Machines)

Problem: AI companies could in principle “launder” inference compute by using it for AI R&D-relevant tasks using third-party data companies and shipping back in RL environments, synthetic data, or experiment results.

These are less concerning than Microsoft due to not having IP sharing agreements with frontier AI companies (now)

Our preferred proposal is:

  • Restrict new IP sharing agreements (limiting the effectiveness of third-party research because they can’t directly build on the frontier AI company’s IP, thus limiting this as a workaround to pacing).
  • Identify external AI/data companies via KYC.7As a BOTEC for the scale of data generation: Claude estimates the current total (Q3 2026) ARR for AI data companies as ~10B$. Let’s say this is ⅓ Anthropic, ⅓ OpenAI, ⅓ everyone else. We can estimate Anthropic and OpenAI current annualized compute spend at 2$ / H100e-hour * 1e4 hours / year * 3e6 H100e = 60B$/yr. So frontier AI company data spend is only ~1/18th of compute spend.
  • Count external compute served to data companies as part of the R&D cap.
  • Auditors conduct ‘data provenance’ audits to check that data generation is happening either internally or via valid data company contracts.
